reviews.author: SilentDawn
reviews.text: The multitude of moments containing potent bursts of pure evil and sorrow are almost too numerous to count, but each one adds up to something of a vivid nightmare. The harsh rattling of chains against the inky blackness. A piece of paper letting off small fragments of light in order to fight the hatred. The squishing disparity of mud as it struggles to keep a man alive. A shot of the moonlight hopelessly trying to illuminate a sexual assault, but to no avail. 12 Years a Slave is dedicated to revealing horrifically malicious behavior that happened to be considered civilized. It succeeds.

reviews.text: Having failed to see this movie before the 2016 election, I've put off getting around to it owing to my immense, eye-rolling aversion to the insistence of retrofitting every political piece of American culture, no matter how old, to be "about Trump." Yet there's actual truth to that charge here, albeit not, perhaps, in the way people think. Yes, Lonesome Rhodes is a vulgar brute, a snake-oil salesman who uses a cornpone, man-of-the-people image to mask a purely mercenary narcissist in it for the attention, but the film also pointedly contrasts him against his cultural counterweight, businessmen whose stuffy "dignity" barely hides the same base impulses of control and greed. What A Face in the Crowd posits with shocking insight…

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: It's hard to review a movie like this in terms of its theme, as so much of it was simply spelled out for the viewer. This isn't entirely a flaw, but the tragic rise and fall of Lonesome Rhodes pretty clearly depicts the costs of fame, manipulation, power, and so on. It's a bitter and cynical soul that it lays waste to, eventually, and it suggests baldly that this is what America has become. It's a warning and a cry for help.

reviews.text: A Face in the Crowd is like standing alone in a crowd and finishing a cigarette in under a minute, then light-headedly glancing at the last cloud of cigarette smoke, wondering where it all went wrong. It is like thinking 'ahh, screw it', and moving your nicotine-caked fingers to take a new cigarette out of the pack, only to realize that it was your last one. The wings of the American Dream can lift you only so high. Your career will soar, but the person you once were will slowly wither inside. Money and fame's charming glitter will fade to expose the naked rottenness underneath, and you'll suddenly be afraid.

reviews.author: Ben Hibburd
reviews.text: Wow...I'm utterly speechless. I don't even know where to begin with this review. Ben Wheatley's metaphysical arthouse masterpiece is a raw, intense, surreal visual feast for the eyes. "A Field in England" is what I consider to be a pure cinematic experience. Set during the 17th-century English civil war, four weary deserters come across an alchemist (played with menacing gusto by Michael Smiley) who's looking for buried treasure in a field that may or may not have supernatural powers. I’m not going to explain much more about the plot, firstly because this film works better going in fresh, and secondly, it’s completely irrelevant to what the film is truly about.

reviews.author: Eli Hayes
reviews.text: Positively one of the most well shot and well directed films I've seen in a long time, communicating a sense of insanity and surrealism within every single scene. It's almost as if Tarkovsky returned from the dead to possess Wheatley's body and direct an English black comedy in 2013, but not quite, because the cinematographic feel is, just... different - many more close up shots, greater attention to detail and less visual metaphor, but it was, at least for me, somewhat reminiscent of the great late Russian master (the use of fog, blowing wind, and so on).

reviews.text: It comes as no surprise that the party scene is the most controversial scene in the film. It is, after all, a moment in which an entire film's worth of quiet contemplation gives way to a flowery, pretentious monologue about nihilism. I can see how that would be jarring and ultimately unnecessary as a stylistic choice, but I deeply disagree with all of the criticism I've read that tackle it from a more philosophical perspective. It's not that I agree with the monologue's content; it's more so that I view the entire film, and especially everything that comes after that monologue, as a strong and deliberate refutation of everything the guy argues for. The fundamental theme I take away from…

reviews.text: A beautifully rendered story wrapped around a deep human truth. Patrick Ness' script (based on his own novel) about a boy who encounters an ancient tree monster is really about coping with the death of a loved one, and packs an emotional punch that is real, honest, and earned. A gorgeous example of how we can use stories to guide us through the hardest times in life. I love this movie.

reviews.author: George Carmi
reviews.text: A Monster Calls explores anxiety, isolation, and sorrow in a depressingly realistic way… a way that can ring true to anyone, regardless of what the viewer may be experiencing internally or externally. Whether it’s tales of loneliness or themes of grief and mental decay while staring illness and isolation in the face, we explore the importance of an outlet… of a means to a release of pent up stress and panic. This film reminds us that having someone to talk to is crucial in times of hardship, and internalized apprehension and worry will only lead you down a dark path… one that may be tougher to navigate out of than you think.

Telling the truth and expressing our feelings is not a crime, and in one way or another, we will find a way to get back at ourselves for not being enough. But we're enough to do everything—never doubt that. It's a great message and an excellent film.

reviews.text: Roger Moore's last Bond movie. This has a reputation for being one of the worst of the series, mainly because Moore was a little long in the tooth at this point. And it's true: he's 58 here, and looks older. In fact there's a scene early on where Bond, M, Q, and Moneypenny are all at the racetrack together dressed in their Sunday best, and it seems like the median age of employees at MI6 is about 87. That said, if you can get into the spirit of an elderly-looking Bond, I actually think this is one of the better Moores. You've got that great Duran Duran theme song, Walken and Grace Jones as villains, action set-pieces with lots of…

reviews.author: Matthew Christman
reviews.text: I remember the exact moment in Adaptation when it went from being a great movie to one of the my all time favorites: the low speed car chase between the Kaufmans and Susan Orlean. This was the moment I realized that, after two acts spent carefully creating rich, interesting characters and struggling with the difficulties of creating truthful art, writer Charlie Kaufman and director Spike Jonze were going to intentionally set fire to the whole construction with an empty Hollywood-style action ending. It's a ballsy move, and it pays off handsomely: not only does it cut the Gordian knot of the how to deal with the tough subject matter, but it's also a point blank indictment of narrative cinema's inherent limitations. Combine that with Nicholas Cage's last known unironically good performance, and you've got the makings of a post-modern triumph that manages to express real emotion while also undermining the Robert McKee screenwriting model.

reviews.author: Sean Fennessey
reviews.text: No one makes the quiet stuff loud quite like Kaufman. This time, I was struck by how hard but clearly it works to animate the experience of falling into and out of a good book, how certain passages, pages, chapters can dissolve in your hands, while others stop you dead, and off into a daydream. The anxiety of writing—or not writing—is the loud here, but the reading—of Orlean, Laroche, Darwin, McKee, Kaufman's own words—feels most perceptive. I wish Spike could adapt him forever.

That anger ostensibly stemming from the polarizing reception to Prometheus, Scott’s bold (if a little misguided) attempt at transforming a beloved perfect organism genre classic into an outlet for his own pretentious musings on the act of creation, an area in which Scott posits that the personal, scientific, mythic and divine all coalesce. Looking back now, it’s easier to accept Prometheus as its own contained space story of human optimism being hilariously crushed by God’s random cruelty, but at the time, and even now, many were hugely disappointed…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: World War One was a barbaric waste of human life, just to keep European colonialism and imperialism afloat. All Quiet on the Western Front comes from an era before World War Two, when the consequences of that earlier war were still strongly felt. Partially the film stems from US sympathy for Germany after the war, but it acts as a blunt critique of all forms of war. All Quiet on the Western Front is very critical of those who profit from war, the governments and kings and manufacturers. Here was a war where ordinary people from so many countries were sent to fight just to please the powerful and their geopolitical interests. We must never forget it.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: All Quiet on the Western Front is amongst the most crucial pacifistic assertions ever accomplished in film. Based on the world-renowned novel by German novelist Erich Maria Remarque, it's an unhesitantly frank look at the complete disillusionment of war from the perspective of an optimistic and loyal young soldier in the trenches of World War I. Lewis Milestone directs with some fantastic tracking shots extending directly across the lines of the trenches, and the many layers of soldiers about to be commanded to rush forward to almost certainly embrace death upsettingly fixes a realistic and permanent perception of the stupidity of war.

reviews.text: With every subsequent movie, it becomes increasingly clear that Cameron Crowe is only interested in one thing: Finding the least hospitable environment for a romantic comedy, and forcing it to accommodate one. The Seattle grunge scene. The wild world of sports agents. A private zoo. Kentucky. The afterlife. (Though, in the spirit of full disclosure, it’s only fair to mention that Vanilla Sky makes a half-hearted attempt to subvert the genre’s most familiar tropes.) The guy is like a cross between Nora Ephron and Fitzcarraldo, obsessively determined to haul meet-cutes and manic pixie dream girls to unnatural places that have little hope of sustaining them. To that end, Aloha might represent Crowe’s final frontier, and not just because it literally begins in outer space.

Salieri despises his younger genius, but in this scene, even after years of hatred, he is swept up in the genius of his creative process. that’s the kind of movie this is, the one that recognises that the power of creation is one that can alter every experience and preconceived notion you’ve had, even just for a few minutes of song.

To see Salieri, a man who spends the whole film reckoning with his obsession and jealousy for Mozart's talent - talent which he conflates with intimacy with God himself - become an extension of Mozart and that very talent, is so powerful. I'm reminded of the quote from Victor Hugo's Les Mis: “To love another person is to see the face of God.” What you see in that final scene between Salieri and Mozart is not jealousy, not obsession, but love. C'est magnifique!!

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The tragedy of Ralph Bakshi is that he's not a very good storyteller. His best work, that I've seen, is still a flawed piece of fantasy (Wizards, which gets bogged down despite a strong ending), and his worst work (again, that I've seen) is a collection of scattershot, weakly linked ideas. From his botched attempts at The Lords of the Rings to his transgressive beginnings, his work tends to be vastly better visually than it is narratively. Here, the animation maintains those haggard edges that he always gives his characters, rotoscoped or not, and the mix of bright colors dulled and deep shadows contrasted. It's like everything is worn out.

There is the realistically drawn science fiction or fantasy narrative, displaying stories from Tolkien or art connected builds from Frazzetta, and then there is complete exploitation narratives that gives a gritty connection to the "Comix" formulation of counterculture direction. Both are expertly purposed for their worth of things, regardless of which island you land on, making Bakshi a true auteur in the brand of animated film. reviews.author: Frankie
reviews.text: Art as the passing on of dreams and trauma; both personal, and societal. A kaleidoscopic examination of the American way, which only starts to make sense in a snapshot songbook like this. Once pitched as the land of freedom, to finally not be worried of troubles and heartache (a Heaven on Earth if you will), only to find heartaches and troubles never go away, no matter where you are. Any place we call home, any person we call family, any stranger we share a feeling with, any song for the times; it's all simply of a moment. In the scope of things, it's all a flash in the pan, but it just so happens to be your life, and you're gonna live it regardless, and see a lot along the way. So make your dreams happen, before you just pass your shit on to someone, or something, else.

reviews.author: Justin LaLiberty
reviews.text: Bakshi never excelled at narrative, which is seemingly at odds with a generation spanning story of immigration and the genesis and increasing relevance of pop music in america but his visual style is so assured that the images here offer more to say than most dense scripts manage to, resulting in an audiovisual pastiche that feels equal parts MTV and PBS, mixing real-life photos and live concert footage with psychedelia and Bakshi's trademark, scrappy, animation style that makes this feel more raw than it ultimately is (this is a major studio release, after all) -- it's a pretty singular experience in a theater (perhaps closest to The Wall in aesthetic and delivery) and thankfully now at least available on blu-ray which has been a long time coming

Sure, there's plenty of names here you'll recognize and they all do their best but nothing can remotely compensate for how bland and simplistic the writing is. The worst kind of homage is one that doesn't really understand it's source material and American Strays is absolutely in that category.

reviews.text: Absolute hypnosis. The rhythm of the line deliveries in every scene is almost magical. Too many examples to choose from—seriously, I could literally pick any moment—but there's an interaction in the final 15 minutes where something the audience already knows is revealed to everyone else in the courtroom and it still manages to come off just as shocking to us as it does to those in the film. That moment works because the nanoseconds in between every word in this thing feel carefully planned and completely intentional. A brief stutter speaks volumes at one point. This attention to detail reels you in and makes it the shortest two hours and forty minutes you'll ever sit through. I'll say it again: hypnotic.

reviews.author: Todd Gaines
reviews.text: Mickey Rourke as Harry Angel, a 1950's chain smokin' gumshoe private detective, hired by the devilish deceiving devious Robert De Niro as Louis Cyphre, to locate a missing person who owes Mr Cyphre a debt. Harry soon realizes this is much more than a missing person case, and he finds himself the number one suspect in a series of grizzly murders. Harry learns the hard way that sometimes people make the wrong deal, with the wrong person. Angel Heart is from genius director, Alan Parker, and features a moody blues New Orleans jazz soundtrack, witty dialogue, gorgeous cinematography, voodoo, chickens, and a smokin' hot Cosby kid. Now, who wants a deviled egg?

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Alan Parker's great contribution to this was moving it to New Orleans, suffusing it with not just mystery but some good old fashioned exoticism (I'm willing to admit it's vaguely problematic representationally, but still). What's even more fascinating is how much of this predates JACOB'S LADDER and yet with its startling patience and bursts of violence and chiaroscuro, you'd be forgiven for mistaking it as an Adrian Lyne movie. However, unlike JACOB'S, it's a better movie once you know the twist. Lisa Bonet was an all-time great 80's ingenue.

There's really no telling how many more people have seen Niel Armstrong land on the moon in the introduction of this film than have actually pulled the events up on you-tube or elsewhere. reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Atlantic City, directed by French film director Louis Malle, wonderfully avoids any moral judgements in its portrayal of the emotionally injured characters featured within its narrative. It contains some delightful performances from its cast, which includes Burt Lancaster and Susan Sarandon, and is a poetic tale with many allegorical connotations and perversities, sensitivities and parodies. It won the Golden Lion at the 37th Venice International Film Festival and was shot in and around the vibrant backdrop of Atlantic City, with the location providing some symbolic metaphors of its own.

And yet maybe it's within this false sense of…

reviews.author: Rizki
reviews.text: An old Victorian building where croupiers used to throng and has-been stars used to perform stands majestically above the boardwalk, before eventually being reduced to ruins. This is Atlantic City at the turn of the ’80s: a poor man’s Vegas for some, a forgotten Mecca for gangsters during Prohibition, a town past its glory days whose inhabitants, for most of them, can find contentment only in cherishing that very past, because they simply have nowhere else to go, nothing else to dream of.

reviews.author: KYK
reviews.text: No filmmaker fascinates me quite as much as Louis Malle -- in terms of range in style and storytelling. This French/Canadian production from the French director, shot on location in Atlantic City, reeks of America in all its decay and decadence. It reeks of money, too, and cheapness... And dreams rotting away. But there's always a veneer of optimism. Meanwhile, Malle can't help his European sensibilities seeping out... Read my blurb for BK Mag here.

reviews.text: Seeping volcanic miasmas bury the land in soporific tarantula-motion! Murmuring, a shrug episodically falls to the earth like a disappearing deer in a cave-trap. Bear cubs grunt and scamper across the grass, ahead or behind! Amoral, non-interested, distant to immediacy. A gleam shone from cruddy armor, a sky like a blood quartz shattered and not swept. Zones and paths started and abandoned, crossed and held up, all a circular labyrinth, web-patterned, a lure, a diversion, predestination. The Old Gods summoned from their holes only to die into an Age Of Boredom, foretold and only delayed for so long. The Old Gods always dying, never dead, always rising, never risen. Long Live The Spider Sanctuary Hidden From The Eyes Of Men! Under The Cratered Crater Of The Extinguished Volcano! Heed This Warning And Do Not Cross! Leave Be What You Cannot Know! Flee Far From This Place Never To Return! <3 nathaxnne

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: Apart from a handful of solid sequences, this is a pile of reheated leftovers: The same running gags, the same Bond spoofs, the same reliance on catchphrases. Austin Powers had a genuine hook; bringing a dated ’60s stereotype into the decidedly-not-swinging ’90s. Mike Myers clearly decided that the only viable hook for the sequel was reversing that dynamic by sending Powers back to the ’60s. But the flimsy way the movie gets him there is way dumber than anything in the bad Bonds that this movie ostensibly exists to make fun of.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: If John Waters' films were just a touch more serious--not dramas, but just slightly less silly--they would be like this. Absurd, dark, and repeatedly fucked up for little reason other than to be fucked up, but with more of an edge than Waters' work, this film depicts a cadre of awful people doing awful things. I have yet to figure out what separates the films where awful people do awful things and it bothers me and the ones where it makes me laugh or otherwise enjoy it. This one falls into the latter camp (ha, pun?).

reviews.text: I maintain now and always that this is one of the great comedies, a slow burn of greed, cowardice and arrogance that depicts an aristocratic structure that creates arbitrary divisions among European nations united in the absurdity of their power hierarchies. The film suggests that the entire aristocracy of Europe is maintained by interbred families and brazen confidence tricks perpetuated by both pretenders and genuine members of the ruling class. Watching this, it's a wonder how WWI took as long as it did to break out. That it is one of the most rapturously photographed films ever made is almost a mere bonus.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Is this a pathetic male fantasy? Belle de Jour is about a woman completely enslaved by her desires, living for her humiliation. Sex and love are different things, with a process of having sex without love needed for understanding the value of love. This is a film of dreams and fantasies, presented as pretty much the same. It's an exercise in showcasing the sterility of perversion when we are made impartial observers to it. Fetishes are only strange when they aren't our own. You can love one thing and lust for another. In Belle de Jour, the contrast is between virtuous purity and desirable degradation. In this sense, it's a naughty girl beneath a good girl exterior. I ask again, is this a male fantasy?

reviews.text: Dark, weird, and fascinating. Aka, my thing. Buñuel’s filmmaking style has always seemed like something that would be my thing so I finally decided to start getting into his stuff by watching this. Absolutely loved it. Whenever a film ends and I find myself staring at the black screen for longer than I thought, you know it’s a good one. I can see myself giving this a 5 somewhere down the line for some reason.P.S. reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "BMX Bandits" is a 1983 action-adventure film directed by Brian Trenchard-Smith. A director of Australian cult films such as "Dead-In Drive-In" (1986) and "Turkey Shoot" (1982) as well as some American horror venues, Trenchard-Smith easily holds a good base for cult fandom in some circles. While you could say to a degree that "BMX Bandits" might be one of his most family features (the section of the rental store that I can easily seeing someone place the VHS tape within just because of the aesthetic), it's ultimately a category that I wouldn't place the film within at all. Rather, it's more of a completely bonkers stunt spectacular, both ironically accessible to general audiences but not afraid to pull punches.

reviews.text: When I first saw this back during its initial release, I had become fascinated with Spielberg's shift towards a political point-of-view in his later films. (I wrote a piece about this shift for Vulture at the time: www.vulture.com/2015/10/steven-spielberg-politics-culture.html) Seeing it again now, especially on the heels of rewatches of LINCOLN and THE POST, it really does feel like there was a conscious decision on Spielberg's part to pick up the mantle of the kind of socially conscious historical filmmaking Hollywood was starting to abandon in the 2000s.

reviews.author: Michael James
reviews.text: Based on true events, Steven Spielberg masterfully dramatizes and executes the 60s period spy thriller, powered by some smart engaging narrative, brilliant performances, perfect production design and well paced editing. Despite being a heavy dialogue driven narrative, the political tension surrounding the cat and mouse game between both countries make the drama compelling and a highly rewarding watch.

reviews.text: Does anyone remember Ben-Hur? No, I don't mean the 2016 remake. I'm talking about the 1959 version that was (at the time) the most ambitious and expensive undertaking Hollywood had yet attempted. I mean, this sucker was the 50s equivalent of Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings trilogy. With a whopping budget of $15.2 million (yeah, it doesn't sound like much today), the largest sets ever constructed for a film, roughly a hundred people churning out costumes, and hundreds of artists crafting statues and friezes, it was exactly the kind of filmmaking excess that only Hollywood is capable of.

reviews.text: Everyone is at the very top of their game in this endearing farce set in rural Taranaki, New Zealand, around Anzac Day 1949. Despite author Ronald Hugh Morrieson putting Taranaki on the literary map he was never appreciated by his compatriots because he revelled in the seamy underbelly of prim country life. We, on the other hand, can enjoy that rarest of beasts, a New Zealand vintage comedy that is actually funny, from the golden decade of New Zealand filmmaking from the mid-70s to the mid-80s, when anything seemed possible.

reviews.author: Jamelle Bouie
reviews.text: There are big ideas in this movie. The generational legacy of racist trauma, the ways that trauma can embed itself in the ground itself, and the extent to which our world is built on the wreckage of that trauma. Unfortunately, they aren’t carried through the length of the film. By the third act, the ideas are largely jettisoned. What’s left is still a thrilling and terrifying supernatural slasher, but I think the movie could have gone to so many interesting places if the filmmakers had carried through on the premise. Still, I see why this is a horror classic. Start to finish, it’s one of the most compelling movies in its genre I’ve ever seen.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Conveying some happy and cheerful pirate action while at the same time ridiculing the authoritarian British monarchy, this Michael Curtiz directed movie additionally features the first fully symphonic score by the legendary Erich Wolfgang Korngold. Errol Flynn’s mischievous charisma keeps this high seas adventure buoyant, even though perhaps too much time is given over to some unnecessary exposition. It’s based on the 1922 novel by Rafael Sabatini and was the first of eight on-screen pairings, which includes The Adventures of Robin Hood, for Flynn with the brilliant Olivia de Havilland and established him as a major Hollywood star, and he commands Curtiz’s often crammed frame with emotionally broad strokes and an energetic physical presence.

reviews.text: It’s a funny thing, to think of how the past can influence the present without us even realising it in the moment. How our formative years can shape and colour our current tastes in the most unexpected or less than conscious of ways. As a supposed adult who is still defining and discovering his so-called "refined palette”, it’s always something of a eureka moment when I get to point to a new discovery or re-burning flame and recognise its birth. You know, its embryonic stages being those moments when we were young and the brain was still a melting pot of the sights and sounds, voices and colours that would surround us. Where the background to our growing up is…

The type that Flynn would be most known for. The type of films that Douglas Fairbanks Sr. did during the 1920s. Flynn basically filled his spot for that niche in the market, because there hadn't been many spectacular adventure films after sound had arrived up to this point. reviews.author: Adam Kempenaar
reviews.text: My biggest issue with BLOOD — noting the hammy comedic bits and the cluttered climactic sea battle — is how the story is so sprawling that I was never convinced of any legitimate character transformation. We must accept Blood's change from philosophical peacenik to vengeful buccaneer and back only because the expositional intertitles say so... when the character himself isn't filling us in. Too much tell and not enough show from Curtiz, a balance the early silent film director would certainly figure out by the '40s.

reviews.text: There's a great line in The Yiddish Policemen's Union about how the only time Errol Flynn isn't smiling is when he's delivering a joke - the tougher things get, the more he grins. That was fresh in my mind as I saw Captain Blood again, and it really is true. What's also impressive is how firmly Flynn's persona is already established here in his first starring role. The irreverent anti-authoritarian streak is all here right out of the gate, as is the flirtatious chemistry with Olivia de Havilland (could any other screen couple build romantic banter around a discussion of gout?).

The film clearly has its comic sights set on From Russia With Love, an early punch only two years after…

reviews.author: Keith Dooley
reviews.text: Carry On Spying is the debut Carry On of actress Barbara Windsor and, with this film, has instantly become one of my favorites of the Carry On crew. Her look, her line delivery, and physicality elicit pure hilarity. And that hair! Williams and Hawtrey are their usual genius in this jauntily humorous spy romp. Bernard Cribbins, returning after a solid performance in the weakest Carry On so far (Carry On Jack), is a delight her as well. Jim Dale is excellent again (and hot again! Especially in the scene where he’s clean cut and dressed in a tux) in a smaller role. Here’s to hoping he gets a larger role in the next installment. If you’re looking for fast paced zany shenanigans by bumbling spies in the Carry On mold, there’s nothing better than Carry On Spying!

It creates a fully-realized future earth, in which the horrors of the present day, from America's imperial jackbootery to general third world strife and privation, have moved from the periphery of the Western world to the center. reviews.text: For a film that is deliberately set up for audiences to call it dumb or useless, there’s actually a heartwarming nature and intelligence within City Slickers. It’s a roaring, exciting and feel-good 90s comedy that doesn’t want you to do anything except enjoy yourself. With pacing that’s both expeditious and self-aware, the film never takes itself seriously enough for the humor to fall flat. All these men deliver competent performances that both entertain you and work as plot devices, even Jack Palance’s 12-minute Oscar-winning performance shines. All in all, there’s nothing apparently striking about it, but there doesn’t need to be.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: A throwback even at the time it was released, Desmond Davis's "Clash of the Titans" is a mythological tale of swords, sandals, and stop-motion spectacle. Eschewing "Star Wars" era special effects for Ray Harryhausen's hand-molded beasties, the film has a quaintness that makes it memorable. That quaintness, coupled with the film's epic story of infighting gods and the humans they love, makes for an entertaining delight that retains its power to thrill and charm decades after its release.

reviews.text: A proper old fashioned adventure movie, telling the story of Perseus on his hero's journey to save a princess from the wrath of a vengeful God. The story is presided over by a team of Gods, lead by Lawrence Olivier's Zeus, who has a penchant for disguising himself as things and seducing mortal women on Earth - the latest rendevous resulting in the birth of his handsome son Perseus, who he spends most of the movie egging on. Clash of the Titans picks up numerous elements of Greek mythology - various monsters, a winged horse, the river Styx,…

reviews.text: In retrospect, it’s easy to look at something like this and dismiss it as outdated or even strange special effects by today’s standards. But that misses the point entirely. There’s a particular kind of craftsmanship here that really deserves appreciation. For god’s sake, they made this in 1981. That alone is kind of amazing. I only recently learned more about Ray Harryhausen’s stop-motion work, and honestly, it feels far more convincing than a lot of glossy, cartoonish computer animation we’re used to now. There’s a physicality to it. These creatures actually exist in three-dimensional space, and you can feel that weight and presence on screen. This is quintessential Troma trash - as in yer face, offensive, stupid and gratuitous as possible but with its tongue so firmly in its cheek that it's unthinkable that anyone would actually be offended by it. Like Dungeness, the Tromaville sky line is dominated by nuclear reactors and the high school sits directly in the power plant's shadow. When the waste management system springs a leak and neon green effluence seeps into the water supply, it doesn't take long for everyone to go full mental, starting with the coke-bottle bespectacled nerd who accidentally imbibes blue green sludge from the water fountain and promptly turns into gibbering, slime-spewing ghoul before jumping through the…

reviews.author: cult_vegetables
reviews.text: The residue of the spandex generation distilled into cartoony Quincy Punks and ridiculous nerdniks. A mutant invasion by the nuclear plant, Troma's classic is a cheerfully self-aware Mad Magazine universe where prop humor and slapstick excess rule. A refreshing blast of nostalgia - completely non-PC, and like early Waters, it's charming as it aims to offend. The film does slide into a more conventional horror goo-fest which dampens the manic buzz. The score, per usual, that trademark tinny hard rock lite.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: While some of the action sequences are utterly ludicrous, this is a good deal smarter and far less jingoistic than I remembered or expected. The film’s true villains aren’t the drug kingpins who set the plot in motion; they’re the image-conscious, war-hungry bureaucrats in the Department of Defense who instigate an unauthorized war in Colombia, along with the President of the United States who tacitly authorizes the scheme. If the past few years have taught us nothing else, it’s that an ending where a morally-righteous crusader tells the truth and brings about some kind of sea change in government is pure fiction. Still, the cynical view of the military-industrial complex here is like something out of a paranoid 70s thriller rather than a stolid ’90s blockbuster, and that’s not nothing.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Endlessly, beautifully committed to loud, nasty violence, never missing a chance to beat the hell out of its hero and leave a bloody mess of his enemies. Lithgow makes a terrific villain, totally having a blast matching Sly's every punch with a terrible quip. Bench-pressing a guy onto a stalactite has to be one of the all-time great action movie kills. No contrivance is omitted in its pursuit of cheap thrills. And then there's the fantastic late-analog spectacle. Literally every trick in the book is deployed here, from (outstanding) matte-paintings to miniatures to rear-screen to good old fashioned practical stunts. It's Bond level, really a superb technical achievement. The plane-to-plane transfer sequence is worth it alone (and essentially remained unequaled until THE DARK KNIGHT RISES). Harlin's best movie in a walk.

reviews.author: Matt!
reviews.text: Free Solo meets Four Loko in this 90s Stallone action classic (which feels more like a product of the 80s than it does the 90s) where sad boi Sly mopes around a snowy mountaintop before getting tangled up with murderous psychopath John Lithgow and a criminal crew that somehow actually feels representative of realistic coworker interaction in how much they just can’t fucking stand each other. Sure, it’s a total Die Hard rip-off, but it’s got giant explosions, bloody kills (shoulder pressing a dude into a stalactite is “fuck yeah” incarnate), gorgeous mountain matte painting backdrops, and enough extreme climbing stunts to give cliffheads (is that a term? Idk) a full body orgasm. Plus, it features the sickest mid-air heist ever filmed by a guy not named Chris “Top Dawg” Nolan. As long as you can make it past the low key super traumatizing opening scene, it’s one boss ass time.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Blatantly derivative of Die Hard/Point Break (just about every action movie from this period) yes, but still among the finer practical action spectacles of the 90s. From the real, super illegal aerial heist sequence that Stallone had to take a pay cut to convince the stuntman to do all the way to the climax which has Lithgow's cartoon knockoff villain and Stallone trading fists/one-liners atop a helicopter hanging to a mountain by a thread this thing just glides from survival suspense setpiece to spectacle action to brutal gunfights. And between all the real stunts, exposed muscle and vicious blood squibs it never lets you forget the raw physicality of the premise which makes the danger palpable even when it gets undeniably absurd like Stallone killing a henchmen by grabbing him by the crotch, lifting him up over his head and impaling him on a cave spike lol.

The movie was a bit stupid at times and very predictable but action movies like this one is meant for you to turn your brain off. The opening sequence had some cool climbing and it was great and very intense when the climbers got rescued, but unfortunately that scene wasn’t topped at any point and I don’t like when movies show all their best stuff at the beginning. The rest of the action scenes were still good though and they did some cool stuff with planes and helicopters, while of course also having Sylvester Stallone hanging from cliffs. The characters were good except for some of the badly acted side characters, but Sylvester Stallone was likeable and John Lithgow made a great and memorable villain.

reviews.text: An apocalyptic nightmare of pure brutalizing evil shot and sequenced in intimate, hyperreal historical detail. Unbearable extreme close-ups of its witnesses and beautiful roaming camera moves (ensuring we see even what the characters maybe miss) that in tandem form a series of vivid, unsparing, and surreal vignettes around the psychological experience of unimaginably barbaric horror being made tangible. You can practically smell the mud and fire and corpses, and just like the young boy in this film I too feel like I just aged 100 years in 2 hours.

reviews.text: There’s a scene, quite a simple scene at a glance, where Robert Crumb walks through the city streets, sits down and looks around. We are accustomed to seeing cities in film, even more-so in life, yet the longer we sit in this scene the more we start to see the city through Crumb’s eyes. The telephone poles become eyesores and soon those eyesores create a suffocating noise. The t-shirts and baseball caps become walking billboards complete with logos we can’t escape. The homeless people become harder and harder to look away from, they’re right there after all. Suddenly it becomes abundantly clear how modernization and commercialization have made a horrible mess of things, a mess we are forced to exist…

reviews.author: PTAbro
reviews.text: Dark City is a frustrating mess. Full of borrowed ideas, from film noir to sci-fi, Kafka to Lang, Blade Runner to Brazil, Dark City co-opts aspects originally intriguing and fails to make them its own, let alone present them coherently. It is fractured, tedious, and, worst of all, without a heart. I mildly enjoyed the last act, where a fraction of the directions the film seemed to be going in finally clarified, but with a mind-numbingly wooden protagonist and a final confrontation rendered laughable due to budgetary constraints, it didn't even come close to redeeming the prior 3 hours (technically 80 minutes, but that's how long it felt to me).

And even beyond the incredibly ill-advised studio-mandated opening voice-over that completely dissolves any mystery the film might have, it constantly goes out of its way to explain itself to you while most of the characters have to remain baffled so they can execute the plot. Imagine if you actually had to figure this out.

reviews.text: Raimi fundamentally understands the art of comic books and shoots his film in the same way a comics artist would panel their work. This is the biggest difference in what Raimi does, and the crop of Marvel/DC movies that have come out in the last few years. He isn't shooting a brand or a revisionist take on comics. He is diving right into what makes them work. Visually the frames from an alleyway in a kind of storyboarder's view, the intense close up, the sparse dialogue that appears while always keeping a characters face in frame is all in the dna of comic books. It's as if he crafted this movie in the same way he would as if he…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Pulpy comic book mad science/noir super-heroics meets genuinely tragic Universal Monster horror; everything in here from Phantom of the Opera to The Invisible Man to Frankenstein to The Wolf Man. Raimi has such a genius eye for fluid, animated visuals (crazy how much of this would serve as a test-run for the Spider-man movies, especially 2) that even when the illusion is occasionally broken with a silly VFX shot it's hard to find it anything less than dizzying and endearing. Elfman's bombast is definitely a holdover from the Burton Batman but its melodramatic effect is a bit different when you start throwing in those uniquely gruesome designs and textures from Raimi's splatter days. The kind of movie where Liam Neeson will completely sincerely say "What is it about the dark? What secrets does it hold?" and then proceed to viciously murder dozens of gangsters for disfiguring him. A good one, I mean.

reviews.author: Joe A
reviews.text: Raimi’s visual language is so fitting for a movie like Darkman— a movie that feels like a fusion of the lunacy of Evil Dead and your classic monster movie tropes. Liam Neeson is strangely the weakest link here, but the movie’s willingness to be both a zany superhero movie and a satire on heroes like Batman (maybe more so on their sanctimonious code) is why Darkman still holds up.

reviews.text: What a delightful, strange little movie. A cross between a Universal monster flick and a superhero film—Batman if he were more Man Bat than Bat Man—it hits familiar story beats while distinguishing itself with fun (and offen gross) practical effects and the strong visual style of Sam Raimi. A young Liam Neeson does dark and brooding well, and while Francis McDormand doesn’t have much to do, she gives the material her all. (She also, uh, looks great.)

Sequels should always, always, always aim to evolve ideas set up previously, whether it be social commentary or makeup effects or literally the zombies themselves. In a perfect world, a sequel flips the pillow to the cold side, flexes new muscles, and re-configures what you thought to be possible. Romero's trilogy beautifully follows this through. Each installment is a flip of the pillow.

If NIGHT can be oversimplified into a Vietnam and Civil Rights comment and DAWN can somewhat more accurately be boiled down to a spoof on consumer culture (though that still short-changes it), DAY focuses on things that cannot be boiled down to one or two ideas. reviews.text: This movie kicks ass. I think it's messy and honestly probably a little sexist, but I also think it kicks ass. Bodies and beauty and aging are all simultaneously goofy and horrific and it's fun to see a movie make that so explicit. Really wanted to watch it after (the great!) reviews.text: "Deliverance," John Boorman's stomach-churning and now-iconic observation of the savagery of nature, man, and conscience is a film built upon and defined by its conflicts. The conflict of man versus nature gives way to the conflict of man versus man and, in turn, man versus self and, finally, nature versus man. It is a poetic progression of the how these conflicts and the destruction imparted by human beings leads only to human destruction. Boorman couches this progression in a heavy-toned, chilling adventure-drama, but the thematic poetry of its conflicts is writ large throughout.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Design-wise this is still totally astounding, but that's sort of where it stops. That the found footage gimmick is dropped whenever it's inexpedient isn't so much a problem (honestly who cares?) as it is a symptom of a muddled metaphor (bluntly, incessantly hammered home, I'll add, but that also isn't such a big deal; that's how this sort of issue-oriented sci-fi usually bends). That's a long, stupid way of saying that it bugs me that this movie hangs on an apartheid parallel, and yet the aliens aren't a colonized and oppressed indigenous people but refugees. Not only that but the finale suggests that everyone would be much better off if the Prawns just went back where they came from.

reviews.author: Nick J
reviews.text: A film trying to be an allegory about apartheid and refugees isn't as effective when the refugees are violent man-eating aliens and the only reason the mustache-twirling comically villainous bureaucrat suddenly has a change of heart and wants to help them is because he needs them to cure him of his mysterious "I'm becoming an alien" disease. The first part, the mockumentary about District 9, is captivating because it does a lot to create a what if scenario based on how the world treats refugees, chock full of references and allusions to past incidents in history, but once you see how the plot is set into motion, it very quickly becomes "Boring Action Sci-Fi Thriller #2409." Couldn't stop myself from checking my phone because it's so paint-by-numbers and stopped having anything else to say.

reviews.text: If you don’t think Sal is a racist, you should probably rewatch this movie. His climactic use of racial slurs can’t be chalked up to a lapse of judgement. reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: My memory of the Pasternak is that of a pretty snobby teen but I recall a rather personal, searching story that really embraced both the intellectual excitement and individual hazards of revolution and emphasized political and spiritual redemption in the face of a world that often rewarded those things with harsh brutality. Lean's movie -- and hardly by accident -- is "merely" characteristically sweeping and romantic, not to mention a gorgeous and handsomely mounted epic, but it's also mostly just about a guy who can't choose between two women (the metaphor not unwelcomly more literalized) while war happens in the background, and there's some vaguely anti-Soviet stuff to keep things contemporaneously upstanding.

reviews.text: I love this movie beyond measure. I love its chokingly lyrical (and so very Raymond Chandler), inch perfect screenplay. I love its dark humor, and the absurdity of glamorous Phyllis and anxious Walter skulking around a grocery store so aggressively sterile it seems to come from inside the monolith in 2001. I love the long takes, and the way the austerity of Billy Wilder's shooting style contrasts so perfectly with the labyrinthine language and tale it's recording. But, most of all, I love Walter Neff and Barton Keyes.

reviews.author: Theo
reviews.text: Ordinary reactions to extraordinary circumstances. A finely constructed, blunt passage of time, the rise and fall of power, and generational change. Ben Wheatley’s first, shot in sequence in one week on a meagre 5k budget, seems tame at first, till the killings start and no one’s safe. Intensely black comedy, deliciously absurd and utterly brilliant, delivered with sophisticated wit and eruptions of extreme violence in amongst nefarious chills.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: The debut feature from Ben Wheatley, the director of Meg 2. Down Terrace is a raw crime drama come black comedy centring on a terraced house inhabited by some kind of low key crime family, where a father and son have just being released from prison, apparently having served time as a result of someone grassing them up. The film was obviously shot on a low budget, but the director makes the best of it. The majority of the film takes place inside the central house, which gives it something of a pressure cooker feeling. The cast is made up of a bunch of character actors who each deliver distinctive performances in their respective roles. The drama veers from comradery…

reviews.author: DirkH
reviews.text: Oh. My. God.It has been a long, long while since I have been surprised by a film as much as I was by this one. I knew next to nothing about it and the way this film draws you in and takes you down a paranoid, dark and rather funny, spiral is just unbelievable. It is quirky, off centre and very original. The acting is fantastic, there are none of the stereotypical gangster shenanigans and the dialogue is superb. The thing is, the people inhabiting this weird little niche in the universe are never larger than life, they somehow ring true, even though the subject matter at hand is always far removed from my own reality. Simply loved it to bits!

reviews.author: 🇵🇱 Steve G 🐝
reviews.text: In preparation for Friday's multi-platform launch of Ben Wheatley's A Field In England, I decided to have a delve through the other couple of films of his that I hadn't seen.

reviews.author: ciaran_vallely
reviews.text: A kitchen sink drama wrapped up in the gangster genre conventions. It is pretty typical Wheatley, he is at his best when he can inject comedy into the darkest of subjects. Shooting this in only eight days is certainly an impressive feat, however, it does also highlight some of the movie's short comings. There are a few narrative leaps that make the entire story a little incoherent at times. And the slow pacing plus single location did start to drag and feel repetitive at times. However, Down Terrace is well acted (having a real life father and son play those roles did give the performances something extra), and shows Wheatley's early promise.

This movie opens cold in 1969 by literally dragging a 10-year-old boy to hell after he steals a gypsy’s necklace. Gloves are off, Sam Raimi is telling us, we’re coming out swinging. reviews.text: I hate this expression but in this case it happens to be the truth: Time has not been kind to Easy Rider. So much of its aesthetic, its depiction of freedom and adventure, even specific shots of our two heroes flying down the road on their motorcycles, have become fodder for commercials for banks and life insurance. But what the commercials miss is the heavy cloud of doom, gloom, and fatalism that hangs over almost every scene, with the possible exception of the one featuring Jack Nicholson as straight man to Peter Fonda's world's most laconic marijuana infomercial host.

reviews.author: Wesley R. Ball
reviews.text: A sweeping portrait of the American landscape through the eyes of two 60's counterculturists, Dennis Hopper's Easy Rider is a gorgeous ode to the open freedom of the American way. It's the ultimate road trip film, simultaneously developing its two protagonists and the characters they meet while intermittent segments of folk rock play backstage to colorful shots of the western countryside. Hopper displays an appreciation for the simple lifestyle that many Americans represent, from the mild-mannered farmer to the typical small town residents. The hippie movement that dominated the 60's thought process is also observed here, offering a fascinating inside look at a culture of peace, love, and a ton of unidentified substances.

reviews.text: „Die gnadenlose Jagd“ ist von der ersten Minute an pure Zeitkoloritessenz und man kann den Film förmlich riechen, diesen kalten Nebel über der Großstadt, den Verkehr in den Straßen, die unzähligen wegequarzten Fluppen und all den Schmutz in den grauen Gassen.Passend dazu sieht die Räuberbande, prominent mit u.a. Ray Lovelock und dem großartigen Gastone Moschin besetzt, einmalig kantig und beinahe comichaft backpfeifig aus, was den internen Konflikten des Schurkengespanns eine ganz eigene Note gibt.Weiter ist Tomás Milián in seiner Rolle des Zigarren nuckelnden Mieseprims ganz fantastisch und hätte durchaus noch mehr Screentime bekommen dürfen, was sicher auch der Handlung gutgetan hätte, fehlt es der Inszenierung doch etwas an der Wucht eines Lenzi oder Di Leo.Nun, trotz der einen oder anderen Feinstellschraube, an der mitunter noch hätte gedreht werden können, hat Regisseur Massi hier einen schön knurrigen Rachethriller und seinen persönlich vielleicht besten Film gezaubert.Und der Soundtrack von Stelvio Cipriani ist wie gewohnt einfach nur bellissimo!

reviews.author: JSlattery
reviews.text: An obsessive interpol agent, the great Tomas Milian, believes a gang of brutal thieves were also involved in the death of his wife years earlier! Nothing will get in the way of his pursuit of the fleeing mobsters, who are led by Gastone Moschin, of 'Milan Calibre 9' fame! Rounding out a great Eurocrime cast is Ray Lovelock, as a reluctant member of the gang! Moschin is the main focal point of the film, Milian doesn't have a lot to do other than chew his cigar and shoot people, sometimes from a helicopter, which he does quite capably! It's a very routine poliziotteschi, but Milian and Moschin are good protagonists, and there's a jaunty, Morricone-esque score by Stelvio Cipriani!

reviews.text: With an unassuming storyline that observes Interpol agent Tomas Ravelli being set on a path of revenge after his wife is murdered in cold blood by a group of gangsters, Emergency Squad was never destined to win any points for its originality. However, what it lacks in freshness, it more than makes up for in gritty action. reviews.text: There is a basic flaw in Orson Scott Card’s Hugo and Nebula award winning novel. It’s un-filmable. Like Frank Herbert’s seminal Dune, it is completely cerebral. Everything that makes these novels masterpieces are the thoughts and feelings of their respective protagonists. Sure, a skilled actor can show fear and anger, and maybe even shame, but if you’re going to wade into the motivations, it’s going to take a hell of a lot of exposition. Exposition and fast paced actioners usually mix about as well as oil and water. Apparently Card himself wrote several adaptations with the usual result of a screenplay that worked brilliantly … if you’d read the book.

reviews.text: Where the last APES was almost complete rehash and ripoff of the first, this one is a near-total inversion of the original; instead of three astronauts crash-landing on a strange planet, three Apes land on ours. It continues the storyline of the previous two movies (an impressive feat in and of itself given how BENEATH THE PLANET OF THE APES ended) but ESCAPE FROM THE PLANET OF THE APES is otherwise a wholly unique animal; it's not an action-adventure movie, it's a fish-out-of-water comedy. At least until, in typical APES fashion, things take a turn for the dark and disturbing.

reviews.text: I’ve really come to fall in love with this original run of Apes sequels. Are the budgets low? Yes. Can you tell the extent to which the producers have to stretch a dollar? Absolutely. But the performances are rich and the story, especially in this entry, is so compelling, with our Ape heroes attempting to find a place in the modern world and our human antagonists essentially grappling with the “Baby Hitler” question. And for as fun and lighthearted much of this movie is, the final act is truly devastating. Highly recommend you check this out.

reviews.author: Sethsreviews
reviews.text: An total inverse of the original film, while also easily being one of the most character-driven films in the franchise. The first half being welcoming and absurd, with the apes on Earth learning other ways—a truly out-of-place scenario that strengthens the viewer's bond with Cornelius and Zira and their relationship. However, the second half swiftly transforms into a dark, dangerous escapade with infinite political concerns and moral quandaries, akin to the first two films, but with a completely new setting and approach. Given that it's virtually two films in one, the balance between sincere satire and true thriller is excellent, concluding in one of the franchise's most emotional climaxes.

reviews.author: George Carmi
reviews.text: I don't find myself connecting with these films the way others seem to. 1968s film felt game-changing and it was really cool experiencing it for the first time, but these subsequent sequels have felt lazy, repetitive, and almost spoof-ey. reviews.text: I love science fiction. It is a genre of endless possibilities and ideas. The notion of a slow burn, low tech space exploration film like Europa Report peaks my interest automatically, allowing me to step over the fact that it is a found footage film.

reviews.author: George Carmi
reviews.text: My fascination with films that take place in space is rather interesting seeing as space frightens me. Id rather dive the depths of the ocean than be contained in a metal casket up in the sky. That being said, I have such an interest in science fiction. The possibilities seem endless and it’s frequently a breath of fresh air seeing where these stories take you. Europa Report isn’t the strongest entry in this genre of film but it’s execution through webcams and it’s semi-documentary style of filmmaking made for a hauntingly realistic experience. It made for a lot of uncertainty and the constant feeling of dread awaiting for shit to hit the fan. It’s no “Sunshine,” but Europa Report had enough strong elements to make it a pleasant watch.

reviews.author: PTAbro
reviews.text: Europa Report almost breaks free of feeling like a SyFy Original at several points, but seems to have an endless supply of clunky exposition, sub-par acting, or intrinsically false set design choices to bring the whole thing crashing right back to STV-land. To be fair, the production value is marginally better than its cable-TV brethren, Sharlto Copley gives a performance that accentuates the weaknesses of his castmates, and the film does try to insert some real-sounding (though sensationalist and forced at the slightest attempt to corroborate) science into the picture. I want to say it's not a bad movie. There is promise of a good film here, but it takes too many missteps; from the interesting yet poorly implemented chronology, to the frustratingly out-of-place talking head bookends, to the disappointingly predictable reveal. Europa Report gets the frequently awarded "At Least You Tried" trophy, but there's a few too many fundamental planning errors here to make a return trip ever necessary.

reviews.author: Tasha Robinson
reviews.text: The latest in the "recovered footage horror story" genre is fairly close to the film requested by people who loved Danny Boyle's Sunshine until it abruptly turned into a slasher movie. Europa Report isn't as beautiful as Sunshine, though it does have high production values for a found-footage film. But it does follow a tack similar to Sunshine, with a group of scientists and crew on a manned space mission, encountering severe difficulties and a breath-stealing terror. And like Sunshine, Europa Report is smart and savvy, mining its tension from a non-chronological but progressively escalating storyline, featuring space explorers who act like professionals and don't make incredibly stupid decisions to advance the plot. This film is simple in retrospect, but thrilling in the moment; it's a good film to watch in the theater rather than at home, to minimize distractions, shut out the world, and get caught up in its creepy spell for a little bit.

He's helped develop the Colonial Marines, the crew of the Nostromo, Reggie and Jack, Frank and Jesse, The Driver and The Detective and Spencer and Reece. I could go on and on. When Walter Hill is involved with a movie via director, writer or producer; the characters don't get overlooked. Extreme Prejudice is no different. It's a modern day western with a lot of Sam Peckinpah flavor. A Texas Ranger. His former best friend and now drug lord of Mexico. A woman caught between them. Both are forward-motion action films that turn on the relationships between single-minded cops and criminals, and the breakdown of loyalty in the name of survival. So focused, both nevertheless capture in a kind of ecstatic truth the collision of bad domestic and foreign policy into one inherently volatile trade, drugs, the perpetuation and crackdown on which heightens traditional genre terms before ripping them apart. The final showdown between Powers Boothe, the devil in white, and the black-clad enforcer Nolte is an exercise in frustrated expectation, a…

reviews.text: It’s official: Pixar is corrupting our children. Thanks to “Finding Dory,” a new generation of impressionable kids — many of whom were too young to be properly indoctrinated by the mediocrity of “Cars 2” and “Monsters University” — will grow up thinking that sequels can be good, natural things that shouldn’t be protested against on principle (it’s “Adam and Eve,” not “Adam and Adam 2: Genisys”!). These innocent souls are too sheltered to appreciate how much of an anomaly this is in a year that’s already punished audiences with blockbuster cash-ins like “London Has Fallen” and “Alice Through the Looking Glass.” But now, thanks to the monsters behind Pixar’s latest and best sequel in years, the leaders of tomorrow across the world will come of age with the delusional belief that sequels aren’t de facto cash-ins, but rather films that are capable of retroactively adding new dimensions to beloved originals.

Ryan Phillippe, Jesse Bradford and Adam Beach play the three men lofted to American Hero status which they in privacy refuted (they were just trying to not die during combat), for them they just wanted their veteran stories of confusion and anxieties heard. The U.S. military wants to use the boys as shills to sell war bonds while the typical American media machine wants to print the glossy legend of plaster saints, not dissect the gory details of the war.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Far too discursive and under dramatized to be Eastwood at his best, but he has always been very good at movies on images even if Haggis script spell things out too much (Ang Lee's Billy Lynn covers a lot of the same territory with less highs, but less didacticism). The combat scenes feel strangely off (I wonder if the main reason he set out to make Letters From Iwo Jima was because he felt a physical dimension was missing here), but his single mindedness pays off as this might be the most melancholic World War II movie ever made, all about waste. no victory in sight. By now, Eastwood has inherited two war projects that started out as Spielberg films…

It was still an interesting look into how the publicity negatively affected those that held up the flag in the photo, but it glossed over much of the fighting, which I suppose is the point Clint Eastwood was going for with this one. I’m hoping Letters from Iwo Jima is the better of the two.

Bright, silly, tonally buoyant, yet wholly adventuresome, this Flash is a cinematic comic book through and through.

reviews.author: Alice Stoehr
reviews.text: A moonlit lake divides a pair of boarding schools in this tender '60s-set romance: one full of proper young women, the other horny boys. Across this lake, two outcasts find forbidden love. Danny, played by Noah Taylor, is too smart, not athletic enough, and hence the object of his peers' bullying; Thandiwe is from Uganda, so she's the butt of racist jokes which she wryly deflects. Thandie Newton plays her as precocious and no-bullshit, yet still very much adolescent, still with a bit of a silly streak. Together, these two make forays (both intellectual and physical) into adulthood, curfews be damned.

Directed by Leonard Nimoy's son Adam, it features interviews with all that were close to him with lots of wonderful anecdotes and info that fill in the gaps in public knowledge of him. It's an all access pass as we see private photos and videos of the man and his family and it's all very personal. I loved when the interviewees referred to him as "your dad" (to Adam). He's not Leonard Nimoy the famous actor to his family. He's dad. While he is Spock to most of us, this documentary shows that he was so much more than that.

reviews.text: This is a fine enough film on its own and an absolutely shocking watch by 1930s standards, but I did not do it any favors by reading the vastly superior original novel beforehand. This lacks both the pathos and the most haunting passages of the novel; nothing here even comes close to the abject horror of "I will be with you on your wedding night." I also think the "degenerate criminal brain" element of the plot is one of the worst adaptational changes I've seen in anything. It was pretty epic when the unloved lab experiment finally made his first friend in a little girl named Maria though

reviews.author: Ben
reviews.text: The Wolf Man needs a hug. Larry Talbot spends the entire movie begging for death. I think that’s why his character is my favorite of the Universal monsters. His anguish feels real. He actually seems to be cursed with his evil. What a fun team up. Bela Lugosi’s portrayal of Frankenstein’s monster leaves a lot to be desired, but he comes around in the finale. This was very much an extension of the lore of both titular characters rather than a shameless sequel. The atmosphere of Frankenstein and The Wolf Man both shine here. The pair were a match made in Heaven. What really tickles my fancy is that these films know how to end. You have a big spectacle then you fuck off. No 15 minute epilogue. With that…THE END

reviews.text: The first of the Universal Monster movies to feature more than one creature in the same film. Frankenstein Meets the Wolf Man serves as both a Monster Mash and a direct follow up to The Wolf Man, as the story mostly follows Lawrence Talbot's arc. A great opening scene sees The Wolf Man inadvertently awakened by graverobbers. He's immortal and not very happy about it, so he hatches a plan to try and track down Dr Frankenstein so he can uncover the secrets of life and death. It's a baseline plot but it serves its purpose well enough. Lon Chaney Jr is great again in his Wolf Man role. He brings a real palpable sense of tragedy to the character…

reviews.text: Unfairly labeled a horror film by audiences at the time (because pre-Code movies were just a different breed), as well as being extremely progressive even by today’s standards, the only real freaks in Tod Browning’s Freaks are the ones who are horrifying on the inside—not the outside. Straightforward, lovable, heartbreaking, and with one of the most satisfying endings in film history. I would literally take a storm of bullets for Hans and Freida.

reviews.author: esther
reviews.text: The word "visionary" means little outside of marketing wonkery these days (did it ever?) but it's hard to argue that Gods of Egypt shouldn't grant Alex Proyas the superlative. Because, well, dude's got a vision. A goddess' luxurious wings turn to flat stone when severed. Another is ripped by a dozen black hands into the underworld the instant she removes an enchanted bracelet. There's a pyramid in constant motion, the sands of its interior shifting to form and unform and reform staircases and pathways. There's a specificity to the movement of this world that can only come from a director with genuine imagination.

reviews.text: Good Night, and Good Luck, directed by George Clooney, is a class act from start to finish. Robert Elswit's scrumptious cinematography provides the allure for a film that otherwise might bore some, especially since the screenplay gets straight to the point, causing the film to be completely devoid of heightened tension. Clooney takes a layered and matter of fact route with this iconic story of Edward R. Murrow and Joseph McCarthy, using a cracking script and a massive cast list of dedicated performers to sell every moment. David Strathairn is the highlight of the whole film, with the main broadcasts conveying an impressive amount of fear and historical importance.

reviews.text: McCarthyism is a ridiculous and disgraceful part of history, yet forms of it still persist to this day. Good Night, and Good Luck. is a fascinating look at its existence and the media reaction to it. The media has a lot of power, which is why an extension of McCarthyism involves targeting and coercing the media. As the film makes clear, everybody censors, but what the media chooses the censor has the greatest impact of all. The media can fight power or it can be subservient to power, or indeed subservient to only ratings and profit. reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Written and directed by Erich von Stroheim, from the Frank Norris novel McTeague, Greed gives an early cinematic vision into the inherent monstrosities often found within the soul of humanity. It regrettably survives now only as a two hundred and thirty-nine-minute reconstruction with still images, from its original length of over nine hours. Still, even in this jigsawed version, the visuals and storyline create a considerable impression which is unceasingly melancholic in its illustration of moral unpleasantness between its meticulously observed characters after a surprise lottery win motivates unfavourable consequences.

reviews.text: A moral tale on the hypocrisy of punk rock music. Limbs only become severed and throats only get slashed when they chase a dollar and lie in bed with nazis. There's a possible point to be made about playing an anti-nazi song in your setlist, but you're still taking their money. The posturing of the stage makes them decry capitalism and public figures, but they run towards the arms of police officers when their world starts to crumble. Green Room is very specific in how false their punk beliefs are when challenged. There really isn't any empathy or much humanity in this movie, but Sauliner wraps his hand tightly around the throat of viewers and there's a kind of sick joy in seeing and feeling blood, steel and death on the cusp of your very fragile body.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: More a fascinating anomaly than particularly good, this one roasted in the fires of development hell for years; apparently they squashed four different movies together, one for each quadrant. There's an arch, self-consciously irreverent attempt at deconstructing a superhero film. Then you have the Superman "among us but not one of us" integration attempt. Third, there's the straight-up FX-driven action film, and finally a love triangle (two sides of which are immortal). Any of these might have stood on their own, but together they hurtle through so much unnecessary narrative embellishment that it borders on total improvised abstraction.

reviews.author: Tyler Ward
reviews.text: Man, this is a film of two halves if I've ever seen one. The first half is entertaining, original, funny, and thought-provoking. The second half is illogical, tonally-inconsistent, and abandons most, if not all, of the interesting narrative threads from the first half. It's very obvious that this is a film that languished in development hell for years before being made.

reviews.text: Firstly, I must apologise for holding off on this for so long. This is remarkable. It’s a film that raises a lot of issues about whether fervent loyalty to the code of honour is more valuable than humanity. And how that is unjustifiable. The execution is masterful, and the pay-off is even better. The resolution is entirely cathartic. It’s also incredibly well-choreographed, touching, and surprisingly exciting. I do think that I will need another watch in order to fully digest everything, though.

Even though there exists a 1925 silent film called The Haunted Honeymoon — considered to be one of the first horror comedies to come out — this is not a remake, neither is it a remake of Haunted Honeymoon (1940). Gene Wilder set out to make a “comedy chiller” that revolved around a thrilling radio program similar to broadcast like The Inner Sanctum.

reviews.text: I never thought I'd enjoy the story of two terminally ill patients quite as much as this. I certainly made me run the gamut of emotions with lots of great, funny dialogue and really tender moments. Edwards, two years after mega-success Top Gun and Dalton, in between Bond outings both decide to do this quirky British comedy and they're both excellent in it. It starts oddly as Edwards attempts to drive Geoffrey Palmer off a cliff; a surprising way to introduce a lead character but once you understand the situation, it quickly settles down. Barry Gibb of the Bee Gees supplies some songs for this (including Diana Ross' Chain Reaction) which does age it somewhat, but that aside it's glorious stuff.

It was a cancer comedy, an odd collocation of terms in 1988, yet holds up nicely in an age where a millennial indie comedy is often more spear-like than slapstick. reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: I really like when a movie is about a character so skilled at what they do it formally opens it up to move with a playfully stylish and effortless ease, even if what that job is the weightiest, matter-of-fact hand-to-hand operator combat of its decade. I think it was rejected on release for taking a genre so inherently exciting and emphasizing the banal savagery of it but that quality is exactly what makes it an interesting entry in the long line of assassin conspiracy actioners. Shame about Gina Carano too because she basically gives a perfect physical performance in this and Soderbergh builds it so well to her strengths it's genuinely insane that he's never tried his hand at this type of action again. Gorgeous digital anamorphic framing, very sharp montage cutting and of course a who's who of wonderful character actors playing slimy human trafficking CIA agents. What’s not to like?

Editing is great, cinematography is beautiful. A nice assembly of talented, high-profile actors and a very solid turn by Gina Carano, who is a great screen presence and an absolute force. I truly believed she could kick everybody's ass. The fight choreography is stellar. The scene in the hotel room with Carano and Fassbender might be the greatest hand-to-hand combat scene in film history.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: In 1982, professional bodybuilder and sometime actor Arnold Schwarzenegger became a bona fide movie star when John Milius’ Conan The Barbarian turned out to be a box-office hit. Why not build a similar vehicle around Arnold’s training partner-turned-rival Lou Ferrigno, who had already starred as the title character in the TV show The Incredible Hulk? Producer Menahem Golan of Cannon Films had been a fan of the Italian sword-and-sandal fantasy films that turned bodybuilder Steve Reeves into a movie star 25 years earlier, so he decided to finance this Italian-made reimagining of one of Reeves’ biggest hits.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: As utterly batshit entertaining as it is baffling, with Mulcahy upping the original’s visual audacity as well as the series’ commitment to being uncut nerd fuel, never caring a whit about logic as it careens from one melodramatic feeling to another, all punctuated by gaudy explosions and spark spewing sword fights. Corporate espionage, sexy ecoterrorists, BLADE RUNNER set design, Sean Connery as an immortal Spanish guardian angel, inter-dimensional hoverboard riding cyberpunk assassins, Michael Ironside psychotically driving a subway train off the rails at 1000 MPH. How something this fun and consistently gorgeous on a lizard-brained level earned such an awful reputation, I’ll never comprehend. It even features John McGinley getting tossed out a window by his jock! Lighten up, everyone. [110 Minute Renegade Cut]

reviews.text: What a filthy, brutal film, even the heavily contrasted color cinematography seems to evoke a sense of rotting decay and immoral corruption. A cop stuck in a past when things seemed to be less unfair and where honor still meant something, but the fact is that he is also deeply corrupted and confused by his dirty surroundings. We are under Reagan’s sun (or we will soon be), there might not exist neither good nor wrong, but there is still death. Culture is prejudice and adultery and the economy is murder and uneven conditions, social inequality goes beyond money, it deprives you of your name. Such an angry film, Aldrich surely got some political ideas from Losey when they worked together.

The audience is forced to endure the assault of a near-constant barrage of surreal imagery that ranges from loathsome to utterly revolting as a rudimentary narrative about a man (George Shannon) on the run from the authorities after the death of his mother (Emmanuelle Riva) unfolds. He seeks refuge in the desert and crosses paths with a weird hermit (Hachemi Marzouk). They eat rose petal-wrapped goat shit together and eventually fall in love. The Notebook (2004) pales in comparison. Arrabal is somehow further left field than Jodorowsky. I might have appreciated this more when I first discovered the Panic movement but I doubt it. Just gross.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: 1950. Two genre-defining noirs follow Hollywood's postwar darkness to its logical conclusion by setting their stories among Tinseltown's decayed soul. Sunset Boulevard is one of Billy Wilder's expertly crafted closed loops, a vision of Hollywood as an empire not merely in decline but founded upon an ideal of constant obsolescence, locking its brightest luminaries into grotesqueries of opulent rot as fame left with age. Nicholas Ray's In a Lonely Place, however, is open-ended, going so far as to abandon its original tidy, if nasty, coda in favor of a grim ambiguity that suggests cycles broken into new and even more terrifying iterations.

reviews.text: "Inception," at its most basic, is two things. It is a heist film dressed in science fiction conventions; and it is a study of a man trying to free himself from a near-suffocating past. "Inception," at its more complex, is a cerebral pop-masterpiece. It is an enthralling combination of thought-provoking, layered story-telling and sumptuous aesthetics enhanced by near-flawless editing, sound design, effects, and musical score. Driven by a pitch-perfect cast and the confident directorial hand of Christopher Nolan, "Inception" is a brilliant and unrivaled piece of filmmaking.

Argento’s (and Daria Nicolodi’s) descent into supernatural insanity is everything I could want from a film that changes main characters every 20 minutes and tosses narrative out the window—taking the the time to fuck my mind with eye popping colors in every frame of every shot. I’ve often said that one day Inferno will be my favorite Argento film, and that day may be here because I love it just as much as Suspiria.
