reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Every viewing of Inferno is a pleasure! There aren't many films that make perfect sense in their own right and no sense whatsoever simultaneously. Argento's story is carried not through logic but by feeling and sound. A curious girl looks for a key; drops her keys, then finds a key in a secret flooded room under a basement. A letter is carried from New York to Rome by notes of classic music. Time forsakes logic, spanning different periods in different places. The written word is power and books on public display become justification for murder in the wrong hands. Words pump through buildings like blood through veins. Argento's brushstrokes bathe every scene in colourful beauty. It's an experience and a work of art.

reviews.text: Have always loved that this one is basically stripped to nothing but the surreal, atmospheric, disorienting nightmare sequencing of Suspiria. Very little attempt is made to ground characters, most of the story and exposition is either inscrutable or incidental to the situations we’re actually watching and instead, the whole thing is just a series of setpieces—all otherworldly colored lightshows and slow-burn anticipation of bloody, bodily harm—loosely strung together by the basic concept of “evil art deco building.” Ultimately the setpieces are so gorgeous and go so hard it doesn’t even matter to me that this movie is probably pure nonsense. Also always love hearing people react to the sack of cats scene, the hot dog man is a land of contrasts.

reviews.author: Matt!
reviews.text: “Don’t you see? I’m just CRAZY about this store!” I love all genre movies, but I especially love genre movies that manage to take something as homey and mundane as grocery shopping and turn it into a complete nuthouse affair. For a very good chunk of Intruder, all we really get is the routine behavior of young small town supermarket employees restocking shelves, doing inventory, and generally fuckin’ around, but then somewhere a figurative switch is flipped and suddenly everything goes off the damn rails. Severed hands in saran wrap, severed eyeballs in olive jars, severed feet standing in a bathroom stall, severed limbs floating in a lobster tank, a stockboy apron drenched in blood, a detached pair…

reviews.author: Digital Press
reviews.text: An analogy, if you will: Intruder is, for the first act, the 80s horror equivalent of 1976’s Car Wash where we viewers are just sitting in on a day in the life of an ordinary business (in this case, a supermarket) and its staff and customers. Nothing really happens in the first act here but it’s still a trip. There’s something about spending a long time in the same location that does more than introduce us to the characters - we also start to feel “at home”, which for a horror movie is a great way to disarm viewers when the mayhem begins. No one expects to be attacked at home!

Island of Terror sees an attempt to cure cancer go badly wrong when it results in the creation of a bunch of slurping bone sucking monsters that begin to terrorise the local island community. Well, science has its risks I suppose. The local doctor can't even button up his cardigan correctly, so he recruits the help of his scientist friends played by Peter Cushing and Edward Judd. This one follows the usual creature feature formula pretty well, with a slow escalation involving some mystery before the monsters are introduced and then all hell is let loose. reviews.text: This one is a hidden gem that plays with the standard story of scientists unleashing monsters on an isolated village and the survivors trying to figure out the one thing that can stop them. No mad scientists, these - they want to cure cancer but get it wrong and create creatures that will suck your bones out and leave you a bag of blood and guts. These creatures could be straight out of a classic Doctor Who episode, all wobbly green lumps and tentacles, with a cup of Cambell's soup spilling out in the critical moments. Peter Cushing is called in as the expert, but instead of the deadly seriousness he brings to his Van Helsing, here he's downright hilarious.…

reviews.text: I love when a filmmaker leverages the clout and budget afforded in the aftermath of a surprise Oscar nomination. After Fatal Attraction, Adrian Lyne cashed out his golden ticket to make a phantasmagoric conspiracy thriller about a Vietnam veteran mailman with PTSD and maybe something worse. Profoundly dark, especially by late ‘80s standards. This is a source code for Se7en and The Devil’s Advocate and a lot of other Hollywood dalliances with Judeo-Christian concepts of demonic evil, with screenwriter Bruce Joel Rubin’s overt references to Dante’s Inferno and a taste for an unsarcastic Cronenbergian body horror. War Is Hell, etc.

reviews.text: At a certain point, watching the 1943 adaptation of Jane Eyre becomes something approaching painful. This surely has to be one of the worst adaptations of a classic novel out there in the vast world of filmic interpretation. Moves from event to event, unforgivably skipping some (see ya formative Red Room incident), botching others (we don’t even get to see Bertha? Seriously?) to grossly failing to convey or understand the material in any way that would service even a mediocre motion picture. Joan Fontaine brings her permanently pained look to Jane, where characterization fears to tread. Orson Welles seems like he is talking to himself the entire time. He acts for himself, as if unaware that maybe, just maybe, he…

reviews.text: Watching this I was initially intrigued and a little amused, but then became quickly and thoroughly pissed off. What little worth this documentary has as a showcase for Moebius and Christopher Foss's concept art just makes me wish I'd read a coffee table book instead; the rest of the doc, meanwhile, is devoted to telling us how brilliant, how ambitious, and how eccentric an artist Alejandro Jodorowsky really is. I swear, the filmmakers giving him a blow job would've been faster and certainly much cheaper. After 90 minutes of his pontificating, supplemented by hagiographic interviews with fans and collaborators, this supposed Great Visionary of Our Time just sounds like a self-aggrandizing blowhard asshole.

Looking over my colleagues' ratings and reviews on Letterboxd, I see a lot of unimpressed folks, and a fair number who downright hated this thing, and hated Jodorowsky. I find Jodorowsky an absolutely delightful storyteller (the Keith Carradine anecdote! Vitamin E!), but to each his own. Some critics I've read are particularly offended by the documentary's claims that his unfinished DUNE in some way inspired many great movies that followed, like ALIEN and the original STAR WARS. The film makes bogus claims and therefore cannot be trusted.

reviews.author: Justin Decloux
reviews.text: The most autumnal disaster film ever made. The atmosphere is wet, the cast wears comfy-looking sweaters, and no one seems to be in much of a rush. In direct contrast to the Irwin Allen opuses (THE TOWERING INFERNO), the film ditches the "A Famous Celebrity Dies Every Five Minutes" structure to focus on a drunk Richard Harris (Is there any other kind?) and his bomb squad trying to do their job. Anthony Hopkins, Ian Holm and Omar Sharif do good work looking stressed.

reviews.author: Dave Jackson
reviews.text: Juice is a horror movie in disguise. Tupac Shakur fades in from the shadows like Michael Myers. In a high school re-imagining of the classic bathroom mirror gag, he materialises out of nowhere when a school locker door is closed. He stalks and kills, gagging for death and violence. He's a slasher with a gun. The horror vibes already mean I love this, but there's so much more to enjoy outside of Tupac's evil turn. There's a phenomenal score from Public Enemy's production team and a soundtrack filled with amazing tracks. The locations are grimy and shot with a slick early 90s touch. Samuel L. Jackson and Queen Latifah show up. There's a DJ battle. The dialogue is ridiculous and brilliant. Juice is something I can see myself returning time and time again. Maybe next year I'll save it for Halloween.

reviews.text: The debut of regular Spike Lee cinematographer-turned-director Ernest R. Dickerson is a Harlem high school melodrama that with the mid-film introduction of a gun and a crime-gone-wrong becomes a pulpy and brutal morality play horror movie about the cycle of street power, violence and self-destructive desperation that tragically swallows this friend group. At 95 minutes it makes a few sudden narrative and tonal whiplashes (and you could argue the moralizing is a tad on the heavy-handed side) but there is too much to love in here to ignore. reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: The Wachowskis steadfastly refuse to make stale violent power fantasies for teenage boys, which seems to piss everyone off. Here you have a young woman who becomes a heroine not because she picks up a gun or is "as tough as a man", whatever that means, but because she chooses not to have her future determined by class or capital (even if it is space-class and space-capital) or really anyone else but herself, wrapped up in an unapologetically dorky homage to trashy sci-fi paperback covers. It's a dressed-up fairy tale, an intergalactic "Cinderella", except she doesn't win by becoming someone's wife, and if she's ever the damsel in distress it's because she decides not to kill or act selfishly. Plus it has Channing Tatum on rocket skates fighting a lizard man. Not even a hair sillier than GUARDIANS OF THE GALAXY or eight installments of Harry Potter bullshit.

We don't deserve the Wachowski sisters.

reviews.text: Perhaps I'm just a sucker for the hazy, '90s Tony Scott anti-real texture, but every frame of KALIFORNIA is gorgeous; bathed is shafts of light, fog, and drifting dust, making it's hyper-affected true crime trailer park grime come to life in a way that only the best pieces of pulp did from this time period (certainly helps when you have a post-KING OF NEW YORK Bojan Bozelli shooting your picture). The rest is this gnarly approximation of what we'd come to expect from Rob Zombie, as Brad Pitt's fajita grease bathed mega-acting and Juliette Lewis' little girl leftovers from Mallory Knox deliver a a real nasty pair of devil's rejects. Cap it all with a really distant David Duchovny performance…

reviews.text: "Nearly a thousand years later, peace in the Kingdom of Heaven remains elusive."Conflict between opposites, driven by principles and pushed even more apart by an unwillingness to make peace—a blatant allegory between faith and open-mindedness, supported by some of the most breathtaking period-piece visuals of the century, Lawrence of Arabia-esque, you might argue (can’t get a bigger compliment really). always find it so interesting when films like this explore the inconsistencies that can arise from following a god while seeking to bring the best to mankind - the difficult choice between what they believe is courageous and what they believe is the plan given out for them by who they have faith in. Plays out with Ridley's typical formula and feels to be complete in every way - a summation of everything he's indescribably great at. Major major work. Exactly my kinda film. Much to think about.

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: Kiss Me Deadly screams onto screen with an opening scene that immediately alerts audiences to its explosive intentions. Out of the blackness of the theater we see a woman emerge wearing nothing but a trench coat, standing in traffic risking her life desperately trying to hitch a ride. Beginning films with a "cold open" wasn't unheard of in 1955, but it was incredibly rare before the 1960's when TV serials standardized it. This opening would have been startling not only because of its content, but because audiences would not have been expecting it. Finally someone picks her up, and she sobs quietly over the opening credits—which scroll backwards, top to bottom. This creates a fundamentally unsettling atmosphere which tells us…

reviews.text: There are very few things that I respect more than a movie that is unafraid to embrace its own stupidity. Kong: Skull Island has thinly written characters, extreme tonal dissonance, bad dialogue, and a complete and utter disregard for the talents of Oscar-winning actress Brie Larson, but it’s absolutely glorious in its brazen spectacle. Its thin characters and tonal dissonance don’t matter as much because it thoroughly commits to its premise, and it seems like the movie is one ridiculous–but hilarious–visual gag after another. The bad dialogue is all part of the fun. It’s not trying to be something it’s not, and that’s something I appreciate in any movie, especially a nostalgia-laced B-movie blockbuster about a giant ape.

Laika, the independent studio behind morbid enchantments like “Coraline” and “ParaNorman,” has already established itself as a formidable bulwark against the ever-accelerating onslaught of computer-generated 3D cartoons, but “Kubo and the Two Strings” makes even the most painstaking of their previous movies feel like a trial run.

News and reality is all constructed, as characters seek new adventures in a city deemed tranquil and bland. reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: "Liberty. Equality. Fraternity." Is this the France that everyone experiences? The characters in La Haine make a good case for the idea that this three word ideal is rarely reached. They are free, but aren't allowed to upset the system. They are equal, but only in law and not in practice. They are fraternal, but only in a tribal way as other groups treat them terribly. La Haine is a scathing look at the system and its fallout in a way mainstream cinema rarely discusses. It's an explosive dissection of oppression and violence, and relevant to any time or place (within France or otherwise) where a young, urban underclass has formed. It's difficult to not see some minor parallels to…

reviews.text: Four glorious hours of camels walking in extreme long shot. Oh, and also a pretty devastating subversion of the white man's burden narrative, in which a man hates his own people and tries to go native, but is always reminded he cannot, no matter his accomplishments. Another epic on the subject would have ended in a blaze of glory. This one stops in a pool of self-contempt. reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: Always thrown by how incredibly melancholy all four hours of this truly is - beginning with the literal death of a legend as we are then forced to witness one man’s breaking point and greatest regrets. Spoilers (I guess), but T.E. Lawrence’s happy-go-lucky charmer is nowhere to be found by the final reel, as he becomes the very human embodiment of white colonialism and arrogance, thinking he can just swoop in and solve a culture’s problems while simultaneously adopting their identity. In the end, he’s truly a man without a country; a great adventurer with no home to return to, as he helped empower those he once thumbed his nose at, while watching children die and even finding he has a taste for murder. Brilliantly crushing, morose stuff, all lensed by arguably the greatest craftsman of “they don’t make ‘em like this anymore” cinematic epics. [70mm]

reviews.text: Interesting that this ran for four installments and neither of these two things happened: an attempt to "get back to the roots" of the franchise by doing a more serious, violent thriller, or a watered-down PG-13 legacy sequel with no profanity or graphic violence. Instead we have this, which is a consistent delivery of goods, including some of the best action in the series -- that amazing freeway chase with the mobile home display truck and the final fight with Riggs & Murtaugh vs Jet Li being the two best highlights. There's also something wholesome about seeing Glover and (even though he's an asshole) Gibson in these characters after so long, as funny and charismatic as they ever were. Joe Pesci says "talk to the hand" a lot for some reason. Bring on 5!

reviews.author: Deckk
reviews.text: 100-word review: Mel Gibson looks so much older without his long hair. 4 is the best Lethal Weapon since the first one with funny continuity jokes (like Riggs' fondness for dog treats), some of the series' best action sequences (like that random Iron Man opening, the Fast & Furious car chase, and the cool Jet Li martial arts showdown), and Mel Gibson and Danny Glover formidably continuing their comical, yet weirdly heartfelt chemistry. Richard Donner created something special with this four-parter without a real dud; let's hope that the more-than-rumoured Gibson-directed fifth-and-final film won't blemish this legacy.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: Coming in 11 years after the first film in its series was released, Richard Donner's "Lethal Weapon 4" completes the franchise's evolution from dark-tinted, emotionally vivid action thriller to comedy-imbued buddy-cop spectacle exhibiting potent notes of weight. As entertaining as its previous chapters, Donner's film offers heat, heart, and personality; and it caps off the series with character and bursts of exhilarating cinematic electricity.

reviews.author: sirvived
reviews.text: This a decent horror anthology film with a good consistent theme of sex and death all the way through. Though there's no wraparound story, each segment manages to be all very different while being similar enough to feel connected and I'm obsessed with the super gross, torture porn-y themes. These stories are more of drama with bleak elements, which is quite surprising considering its gory poster. Some moments make me squirm and there's a few good chuckles. The film starts with House and Home, the most predictable segment out of three, but still offers campy fun. The second one, Mutant Tool, I'm not so sure. It's a thoroughly mixed bag but it's the most ambitious so got to admire the ambition. I'm surprised at how messed up and bleak the third segment was. Bitch is without a doubt the best one and they save it for last.

But he brings us so much more than just grit and gore. Oh yes, the cinematography is simply spot on perfection, it's a crime that this film wasn't nominated for that alone. reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Beginning the film with a confirmation of the monumental loss of a child the Macbeth's suffer (only ever briefly implied in the text), this recontextualizes their horrifying royal intrigue actions with unhinged grief-stricken emotions and portent expressionism regarding cycles of fated generational violence. All the Tarkovsky-inspired imagery is drop-dead gorgeous of course, but the real power is in how Kurzel uses it not just as beautiful stage direction but to formally move Shakespeare into the realm of dreamlike opera. Muting and cross-cutting the words in favor of huge passions and looming landscapes in a sensorial fog; a primal fury of dirt and blood that eventually gives way to fire and ash. That the anguished mood and madness of this was largely ignored in favor of The Revenant when it came out (which walks the line between being brutish and pretentious far less successfully imo) still personally offends me.

reviews.author: John Wayne of the Internet
reviews.text: Here's another reminder that Dennis Hopper was so goddamn legit. All the rigorous training they beat into him during his early years working for studio system Warner Bros really benefitted a loose cannon like him. Writer/director Philippe Mora genuinely thought Dennis was going to die during the filming of MAD DOG from the sheer amount of substances he was consuming everyday. Thing is though, because of that training he was the type who’d still remember to keep continuity between scenes, while simultaneously being a whole bottle of rum deep with freshly shit-in pants. Working with him would have been a nightmare, but the end results typically paid off. They definitely did here. A super solid entry in Mora’s catalog, and a really impressive first film in general.Also, David Gulpilil and Hopper are an adorably cute pair of best buds.

reviews.text: Mad Dog Morgan is a real mess of a film. It is one of the most notorious of the cycle of 70’s Ozploitation films – due to the amount of alcohol and raving Dennis Hopper did during the shoot – allegedly he had enough alcohol in his bloodstream to be declared legally dead! Hopper was deported from Australia the day after filming had wrapped. Most of the crew were novices - and the joins and lack of experience can unfortunately be seen. It commits the cardinal sin for a film of this type: being poorly paced and overly dull.

reviews.author: Mike Kennedy
reviews.text: Daniel “Mad Dog” Morgan has always come behind Ned Kelly in Australians’ connection to their bushranging history. Their criminal exploits occurred in the same general area around the Victoria-New South Wales border but Morgan was 24 years younger than Kelly. Morgan was sentenced for the first time - six years imprisonment with hard labour for highway robbery - in the year Kelly was born. Morgan was shot and killed in 1865 and Kelly began bushranging as a sidekick to Harry Power as a 14 year old in 1869, so Kelly would certainly have known of Morgan.

reviews.text: A riveting and minimalist action film of bare-bone badassery and primal rage; George Miller's Mad Max is the one that started it all, and after all these years, It still remains one of the best low-fi experiences that you can have. Miller's directing, Cliff Hayes and Tony Paterson's editing, David Eggby's cinematography, and Brian May's score all comes together into a type of visual shock treatment. You can smell the gasoline radiating off of the screen, and in spite of some rough patches with the pacing and some budget constraints, Mad Max continues to be a dazzling ride.

reviews.author: Craig Duffy
reviews.text: Film students and critics love to make a big deal about the "showy" moments in this movie. They go on about the long takes, the prologue, the hidden 82s, the narration, the sing-a-long and the frogs. It's kind of hard not to. And with an epic run-time of 188 minutes, there is no shortage of "showy" acting as well. Not a single moment comes easy. People hurt and people get hurt. Every single character is an exposed raw nerve. So yeah, there is a lot to chew on in this film both emotionally and aesthetically. But I think what brings people back again and again is actually something rather simple. They just like the reassuring message that no matter how bad things get, the rain will eventually stop...when you wise up.

reviews.text: Beautiful movie, and I'm not just saying that because my girl Shelley Duvall is in it. Zsigmond shoots British Columbia the way it must've felt to these people, like the soaking wet edge of the earth. Something I couldn't stop thinking about while we watched was the film lens of nostalgia, how completely it's colored my own sense of how history must've looked. When I imagine Ancient Rome I imagine a Technicolor epic full of senators who look like when we had more interesting looking actors. When I imagine the Wild West I imagine whatever Sergio Leone wants me to imagine. This is 1902 in Washington but it's also 1971 in British Columbia. They're completely different times with different sensibilities…

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: Rintaro's Metropolis is a cinematic oddity. Not to be confused with Fritz Lang's silent masterpiece Metropolis, this animated film is an adaptation of Osamu Tezuka's manga Metropolis. The manga shares some elements of original German film, but Tezuka says he had only seen a still image from it of Maria's Transformation; the anime, on the other hand, borrows more liberally from the original film, despite being an adaptation of the manga, which is not an adaptation of the film. Metropolis (2001) is, above all else, Metropolis (2001), and it is simultaneously both similar to and different from each other Metropolis that came before it.

Metropolis almost seemingly forgoes it's plot about humans, robots, facists, and detectives, in service of a grand vision of an impossibly stunning retro-future city. Obviously, the creators were inspired by the original Fritz Lang film, but the narrative being a mish mash of human rights for robots, unrequited love from a father figure, class wars, and the existential crisis for androids, is definitely Tezuka. reviews.author: Karsten
reviews.text: What makes a life a life? The people who raised you? The places you went? The home you grew up in? The historical events that occurred? The relationships you had? The deaths you witnessed? The philosophies you learned? This film is saying these are all correct, focusing on the idea that life is based off memory. Which then poses the question, is life only based off memory? Is what you didn't remember not considered a part of your life? Told with a visual style that had me literally pausing the film to take it all in, Mirror introduced me to a life so distant from my own but through a lens that felt so familiar. It's silly to think I or anyone is going to figure out the purpose and meaning behind life, but if there's anyone that'll make you feel like you're a little bit closer to figuring it out, it's Andrei Tarkovsky.

reviews.author: Dirk Diggler
reviews.text: Mirror is a poetic, abstract and deeply beautiful film that offers glimpses of memories from a childhood and life of a dying man, and also happens to be one of the most mesmerizing cinematic experiences i've had. It's a non-linear, jumbled, quiet, deliberate and slow film that puts you into a meditative state of mind with it's complex structure, lingering camerawork, dream-like atmosphere, and audiovisual treats. While the whole film is otherworldly beautiful, the burning barn sequence is a contender for the most beautifully filmed sequence of all time. And I was on the verge of tears during the ending. Mirror can be a difficult watch, but it is undoubtedly a masterpiece of poetic and visual filmmaking, a human and resonating film that left me speechless.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: There's a beat at the end of this where Ethan is frantically explaining to his wife how to firmly load a clip into an automatic pistol. "Like the batteries in the flashlight in the kitchen." Abrams isn't a particularly adept visual filmmaker; this is shot largely in close-up and its setpieces coast more on length and sheer ingenuity, with shots strung together for clarity if not particularly composed or edited for any dynamic effect. But it's the tiny stuff here that's emotionally grounding instead of the film squeezing you with setup-release narrative structure (although it still does that sometimes too). In fact, one of the most exciting moments comes about from the realization that you've missed an entire potential action scene. I mean yeah it's a $120 million Alias pilot but I always thought the Alias pilot was a lot of fun.

reviews.text: So much talk about luck and chance in this one and it all feels like the franchise confronting the plot armor of Ethan Hunt’s truly impossible existence head-on– but it works. A lesser series would (and did, in its 9th installment!) try and make a dumb gag of its characters’ god-like inability to face defeat, but lamp-shading it in earnest shows so much more respect for the audience and so much more reverence for Hunt. So much so that by the time he dies, comes back, and literally screams “I am the disk,” it feels both like the least believable outcome and the most inevitable conclusion. He is the alpha and the omega. He is the MacGuffin. He’s the reason…

reviews.text: The premise of Moon is a fascinating one, but I was deeply disappointed by how it developed. The script goes in a direction that feels both underwhelming and bizarrely revealed. It’s an unpleasant twist that doesn't make me feel much of anything besides pity. The passage of time is poorly handled, despite being such a key component of the plot. Direction is equally lacking, with respect to the visuals, action, and overall pace. Sam Rockwell's performance is the only saving grace here. I can easily see this exact same premise being elevated into a phenomenal, haunting work of science fiction. To me, Moon took a rather forgettable approach.

I mean, not even the main cast saves this, since the chemistry between leads is lacking, and any resemblance to Hitchcock's usual visual style and camera work is not found here. The dialogue is lacking, and the story never commits to a solid premise, and a sense of tension is not there. Yeah, it's a shame I'm ripping on it so hard since it's Hitchcock, but yeah, it's pretty crap and entirely unforgettable.

reviews.author: Chris Hughes
reviews.text: Screwball comedy is inherently chaotic. The best screwballs have a sense of danger. As if the rapid fire lines are improved. Hitchcock was fully capable of doing comedy but his approach to film generally was so controlled and calculated that he didn’t really mesh with the screwball genre. Carole Lombard (who’s reputed to have asked Hitchcock to make this for her) looks as good in Mr. and Mrs. Smith as she ever did. Hitchcock knew exactly how to light and shoot her. She’s dynamic, funny and giving one of her best performances. On the other hand Robert Montgomery seems miscast. I just don’t buy the Lombard/Montgomery match. He’s too stiff. Too buttoned down. In the end Mr. and Mrs. Smith is a minor Hitchcock that’s mostly enjoyable as a showcase for Carole Lombard. It’s funny but it isn’t frantic and joke packed like the best screwball comedies.

It’s 1954 and the week when a formerly great, increasingly washed-up star of earlier cinema, Alan Swann (O’Toole), is set to host the show. Its revolutionary genre-creating action sequences are second to none, packed tight with some of the most exhilarating fights that can be seen from watching giant robots fight godlike beings. But the real brunt of the series is behind its philosophical ponderings that boil and intensify before coming full circle in its final two episodes, which were unfortunately constrained (by its budget) into a minimalistic narrative form that gave the series a more psychological ending without offering a more satisfactory closure on the events happening around the protagonist. reviews.text: A raging, haywire and socially anarchic satire that is executed with mythic intensity and entertains as a gorgeous mess. Lumet interprets and masters the vivid idea of when discombobulation and anger meet, that being the state of mind that almost all human beings face, visually and narratively ensuring that it’ll get more intense and prominent with time. Through this, the audience is given a force of calculated instability that runs within the workplace and sees the backstories and personalities of each ingredient. There’s such a damaging, critiquing effect over each moment yet the chaos is what makes it so entertaining.

reviews.text: Fascinating. Inarguably iconic but also actively struggling against its roots as blaxploitation, so much so that it has a really hard time balancing a pretty clumsy cop story with the anger and social anxiety that's clearly on its mind. Nino Brown's SCARFACE narrative has to fight for time with Van Peebles and his crew, none of whom can match Snipes for sheer charisma (no not even Ice-T), not to mention that they're basically ciphers. And the righteous indignation over the drug crisis actually makes pains to paint itself as having little to do with race and more with the simple scourge of addiction. The rest features an almost cartoonish lack of verisimilitude that nevertheless felt entirely "real" at the time. To a lot of audiences this was entirely new territory.

reviews.author: Matt!
reviews.text: Playfully preachy & delightfully distasteful blaxploitation Scarface; a 5-star movie if you were to remove every scene not directly associated with Nino Brown. Seriously, there’s so much shoehorned commonplace detective work, it feels like if Wolf of Wall Street had decided to allocate half its runtime to Kyle Chandler’s character instead of Jordan Belfort. But that’s alright, cause even when it’s brimming with badass swagger and great performances (shoutout Chris Rock, seriously), Wesley Snipes is THAT much more elite than everyone else combined. Dude spawned quotes and memes out the ass for decades to come, and even got to hang upside down like Batman to slit a dude’s throat! I do wonder, though, how good would Nino have been at filing his tax returns?

reviews.text: James Cagney type shit. A remarkable, colorful cartoon pastiche by Van Peebles located somewhere between bleak, socially-conscious crack epidemic studio crime saga ("you gotta rob to get rich in the Reagan era") and gruesome, bad-taste blaxploitation update on classic Warner gangster films, doing for the 90s what Larry Cohen did in the 70s with Black Caesar right down to the unreal NY location work. Even the whiplash of ending your movie with such elaborate production design (all the gothic art deco interiors of their base of operations and empire board room are insane), acrobatic camera movement (those overhead twirls!), and intense, squib-heavy slo-mo violence on a "crime is real and bad though, by the way" card in the credits just…

The most horrifying image in that movie is the red and blue of the police arriving on a crime scene where our hero cannot be seen as such in the lens of the police state. reviews.text: Rather than delivering a straightforward adaptation of the famous Biblical tale that would appease most ultra-religious purists, Aronofsky has crafted a madly audacious and awe-inspiring hybrid of a dark psychological thriller, a gritty family melodrama on steroids, a fantastical sci-fi disaster epic, an environmental cautionary tale and a challenging philosophical parable that poses deep, timeless questions with its themes of morality and sin, faith and hope, revenge and forgiveness. A work of wild ambition, striking artistry and dramatic intensity, Noah intertwines genres and defies expectations with its unconventional storytelling, creative liberties, spectacular visuals and transcendent music score, infusing the grand scope of the flood myth with a deeply intimate and absorbing character study, firmly anchored by Crowe’s heartbreaking performance and Aronofsky’s fearless direction.

reviews.text: The arresting fashion in which Darren Aronofsky injects profundity into a predominantly superficial genre may be the most impressive accomplishment of the resplendent and epic Noah. Aronofsky, a filmmaker with the incessant purpose to innovate and redefine, puts forth one of his most divergent motion pictures but simultaneously one of his most mainstream with this re-imagining of Noah's ark. A true blockbuster on the surface, the sweeping temperament of Noah is uncommonly matched with intelligence and a bonafide, gravitating narrative that elevates this latest Aronofsky venture from a grand blockbuster into a visceral and provocative experience.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Omega Syndrome" is a 1986 exploitative action film directed by Joseph Manduke. Wearing its upfront energy completely on its sleeve, there really no illusion what kind of delivered shlockfest one will get watching "Omega Syndrome". In that you can find some fun in the film if you really accept the pace in which the film is going to proceed at going forward, but still in that energy it holds an odd build. The narrative of it all is an ex-military do-gooder, trying his hardest to assimilate a family driven lifestyle, that is until a belligerent grouping of white supremacists kidnaps his daughter and stir things up. This is when himself and his gun depot buddy with a limp go guns-a-blazing…

reviews.text: Does a great job of replicating the pervy bio-organic weirdness of the cartoon, with vaguely vaginal poison dart-shooting security fruit, spies passing sensitive stolen technologies with their tongues, or Sophie Okonedo's hand-feet. But it was probably a mistake to try to manufacture a decipherable plot out of what was always an intentionally narratively baffling feat of imaginative futurist design and impossible animated acrobatics. There's just too much talking and explaining, and what should be carried off with alluring silence instead seems like intentional camp. That's not necessarily bad, but unfortunately Kusama's action has been sliced to ribbons for a PG-13, and in the occasional instance when it's not, you get bland stuff like Charlize spinning in place with a machine gun, and so most of what was lithe and visceral in the source material ends up a generic blur here.

reviews.text: Very much on brand with Ringu and Pulse, One Missed Call features a great first act, ponders a bit in the middle before bringing it all home. Miike’s atmosphere is always on point throughout, especially during the tension drenched setpieces. Still though, as much as I liked revisiting this it’s very much a straight Miike jam, abandoning his signature surrealistic absurdities which I love so much. That works here though and One Missed Call is quite good, not in my top ten Miike or top Ten Japanese horror jams, but a creepy good tale for the early flip phone generation. The ring tone in this is one of the eeriest things I’ve ever heard and I kinda love it!

reviews.text: In the decades that followed World War II, Japan became a country in transition. A country that wholeheartedly embraced technological advancement during this period of rapid economic growth. A country that embraced the future, perhaps in an effort to leave the bitter memory of the war behind them. To think of Japan in this way, however, only gives us a view of one side of the coin. While they embraced Western culture and technology with great zeal and fervor, Japan was also a country that clung tenaciously to its past, as well as its own rich cultural heritage. What emerged from the chrysalis of that postwar period was a country that existed simultaneously in two periods. Where you could cross…

reviews.text: 100-word review: When you want an intricate, frighteningly realistic pandemic movie, you watch Contagion; when you had a long day, and just wanna watch pandemic-related pulp, Outbreak is what you're looking for. Swapping realism for sensation, Outbreak features a frantic and yelling Hoffman, a deadlier-than-Ebola virus that spreads like the flu, and bombs (Contagion certainly lacks bombs). It's not even truly a pandemic movie, because (spoilers) the disease never spreads beyond a few outbreak (hence the title) locations. It criticises the army's ruthlessness when it comes to the weaponisation of anything that's good at killing people, which is nice.

But to me, this lacked the emotional investment needed for one of these kinds of intentionally confusing and disorienting films to work. Perfect Blue managed to be more overwhelming to the senses AND more emotionally impactful by perfectly getting you into its protagonist's fractured headspace. This, by comparison, felt stretched in far too many directions for me to really connect with anything going on. I also don't really get the Inception comparisons - yes, people invade other people's dreams, but that's sort of where the plot similiarities end. Inception may lack an emotional core to some extent, but it has the benefit of an enthralling clear-cut…

reviews.text: The way Jasper slips in and out of sensory-overload music video direction during otherwise understated, handheld vignettes is not terribly far off from how I experience the world. This story means a lot to me. I love Patti, I love the friendship, I love the music, I love the collaboration, and I love how it sets up its cinematic predecessors (8 Mile and Hustle & Flow) specifically to knock them down and make way for something unique. The climax plays a bit more like a Movie Ending than it originally did—a hell of a lot can happen in eight years—but it’s still very much earned. If the world ended today, she would adjust.

reviews.author: Scumbalina
reviews.text: I didn't live in Paris in the 60's but it's so easy to relate to these bittersweet experiences. Peppermint Soda doesn't focus solely on one sister, but a balance of both. A three year age gap separates them, such a small yet dramatic difference. I appreciated the subtleties between peers. Little glances and shifts. This film has a lilting quality that's just out of grasp. Everything that occurs happens at a very natural pace. You can feel how personal this must have been for Diane Kurys. The problems and emotions are very sincere, though the film shows them with grace and restraint. Possibly the greatest female coming of age film of all time.

reviews.text: Ever heard of a film knocking the wind out of you in the first five minutes? If not watch Ingmar Bergman’s Persona. The opening sequence of this film is surely one of the most unsettling, incredibly haunting things I have ever seen on screen. The music, the images and the lighting are so discomposing to the viewer that within an unbelievably small period of time into the film, Bergman catches us by the throat and makes us experience an almost unbearably intense psychoanalysis of a woman’s mind or is it two women’s minds, I can never be able to tell.

reviews.text: Didn't technically watch it but I did sit in my hotel room and perfectly remember it frame by frame over a sixteen hour period where I was in immense physical agony. At any moment I could've walked away from what I was doing but I didn't do that. I instead explored the boundless potential of the human mind and body acting in communion to complete a task for which neither were designed. Not only did "this task" hurt me the way that waking up during surgery hurts you but it triggered a sort of "anti REM" in me that made me feel like I had been awake for 75 hours doing manual labor with no break. My life can be cleanly divided into two acts now: what came before and what came after. I am infinitely worse off now that I've done this.

reviews.author: Matt!
reviews.text: A special film, and one that I cherish deeply. The darkest, strangest, most human fairytale out there, with the camp and sincerity of a visionary Don Coscarelli determined to wield a $300k budget like it was the riches of King Midas. The entire franchise is just a warm hug of whacko cosmic horror and grounded emotion that few movies, if any, have ever managed to balance as expertly. Watching this knowing the ending and the stories that would follow is truly an incredible experience. And once that theme hits, holy fuck—I am transported onto a different plane of existence. The vibes, the aesthetic, the characters, the iconic moments and objects…for what it’s trying to be, it’s quite literally perfect. I love everything and everyone. No one can rationalize death. The ending is heart-wrenching to the Nth degree. 50 stars.

reviews.text: What if The Day the Earth Stood Still had more zombified ghouls, foggy cemeteries filled with styrofoam tombstones, stock/repeating footage, shower curtains, and dying acting legends interacting with carnival freak show personalities? I’m sorry I can't understand why I’m supposed to hate this. Is it just because the man had very little talent, taste, or technical skill? Matters much less to me than the weirdly imaginative and barely strung-together charm of his old-timey vision of sci-fi horror. Ed Wood has such an obvious passion for a dead type of Hollywood movie he grew up on and his desperate attempt to re-animate it with every bizarre, meager Halloween store trick he knew is sort of beautiful. "Future events such as these will affect you in the future."

reviews.text: More than anything else, 'Point Blank' reminds me of an Anglo-American analogue to Seijun Suzuki masterpieces like 'Branded To Kill' and 'Tokyo Drifter'. Discontinuous sound/image mapping, reflections in reflections, shadows framing shadows. Everything bought and paid for and sold out. Lee Marvin is both an agent of vengeance and a patsy, corroded and obsolete in the face of modern management techniques. In a world where corruption is the status quo, befuddlement in low-level thugs is confused with honor. John Boorman's run of straight ruling everything up through at least the mid-eighties begins right here, as well as giving himself over to a corpus of films without a solution wherein every attempt to do so only digs further inside.

reviews.author: Rizki
reviews.text: Jean is a man of few words, but his demeanor and his clothing speak loudly enough about his condition. He’s dressed as a soldier and aimlessly wanders somewhere outside the city; he’s at the edge of the world and at the edge of himself. Although the word is never uttered in the film, the innuendo is obvious: he’s a deserter. He isn’t proud of himself — certain circumstances might have pushed him to it: malcontent disillusion, some existential sickness — but the film doesn’t give him excuses or alibis. His desertion isn’t the end of the journey, but the starting point. Or is it?

reviews.author: James (Schaffrillas)
reviews.text: For all of its famous and well-documented faults, it's impossible to deny how thematically ambitious and rich this film is as a standalone story and a piece of the larger Alien franchise. Undeniably pretentious and heavy-handed with many illogical moments to be found, but weirdly beautiful and captivating at the same time. As grand from a directorial standpoint as you would hope, with enough heart pounding sequences and existential dread to overcome my initial skepticism of how much I could really get out of a mostly Xenomorph-less Alien movie. For being one of the most divisive blockbusters of the 2010s, I definitely wasn't expecting to come out of this one on the side of its fans. I think it's pretty good! Who knew?

reviews.text: Mismatched adventurers race bad guys to a rumored treasure out in a distant land. Surely there are other types of stories to tell in the genre, but not according to this, "Raiders of the Lost Ark" (also '81), "Sphinx" (also '81), '85's "King Solomon's Mines", and so on. How well do they pull it off this time? Averagely. It's spirited, scenic (filmed and set in the mountain ranges of New Zealand) and you may already like one or more of the three leads - Donald Pleasence, Lesley Ann Warren, Ken Wahl - but also light on characterization, runs a low-rent series of plot machinations, doesn't aspire to cool action or set pieces aside from extensive helicopter stunts that get repetitive…

But, unfortunately, word has gotten out of his find, bringing treasure hunter Theo Brown (George Peppard) and his gaggle of goons to New Zealand, seeking quick cash.

reviews.author: Schizopolis23
reviews.text: This underrated and under seen movie needs a blu-ray release. Breathtaking helicopter chases through the mountains of New Zealand. A kinetic speedboat chase. All scored to Brian May's bombastic orchestra, pre-Road Warrior. Simple action-adventure story. Local working class father and daughter along with an American expatriate go on a treasure hunt against greedy corporate mercenaries. One of the best scenes in the movie was an unexpected night of drinking and singing with the local Kiwi farmers. By morning, the farmers transformed the trio's wrecked helicopter into an all-terrain tractor. Locals stick together.

reviews.text: titane takes everything this does and turns it up a notch, which i thought would make this weaker on a rewatch. but instead i’m only more impressed with how ambitious and thematically dense this is for a directorial debut. love the idea of going to vet school, watching how humans treat other humans like animals in the literal first “hazing” scene, being repulsed at how your classmates just casually eat meat, and being like…well this finger is no different than a meatball, if that’s how this is gonna be. the score being mostly instrumental organs, genius. i love the way ducournau shoots her movies; harsh shadows, bold and bright colors, making skin look meatier than it should. and above all such a unique coming of age story, rebelling against your family only to realize it was in your blood all along, amazing. will always suffer through a stomach ache for julia ducournau 🩸

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: I kind of have to choose to tune into this wavelength whereas some folks are either adamantly against it or instinctively with it. To me it's so packed with incident that it feels like its immersed in a complicated continuity but really isn't. Instead it's blissfully anti-narrative, contrived successfully to hop from fight scene to fight scene without a lot of filler. And why not? That go-here-do-this-now-fight structure coupled with Anderson's symmetrical compositions and action-pose frames somehow give it the dramatic weight of the cut scenes I used to get so wrapped up in when I was deep in a great game, where every narrative beat was played like it was the most life-altering development imaginable.

reviews.text: Rififi might be another entry in the gangster/heist genre, but it's certainly the one that consolidated it — elevating robbery to a level of artful craftsmanship and portraying thieves not as honorable human beings, but as individuals bound by a tacit code of honor that fascinated viewers who remained on the safer side of the law. The film established the archetypes that would shape the plots of future caper classics. Just one year later, Kubrick released The Killing, adding a layer of originality through clever editing and precise timing.

reviews.author: Harry Ridgway
reviews.text: A motion picture of unique softness in a genre habitually packed with unyielding brutality, Road to Perdition subverts the gangster mould with its prodigious heart and motifs of retribution and bondage firmly inscribed in the nucleus of the film. The picture glows with intimacy, a focal point in the works of Sam Mendes, whose grip on families confronting desolation is second to none and is the vanguard of the canvas here. All characters apart of the mob know and believe their only true destination is perdition; they're born, they work, they have a family, they perish. Road to Perdition speaks of a story where one man decides to contravene this unanimous law and break away from the system for the…

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: Caught contentedly between The African Queen and Peter Pan, Romancing the Stone is less a Raiders of the Lost Ark clone and more a "what if Indiana Jones happened to you?" kind of adventure. It's all pulpy throwback, but Zemeckis keeps it lively and fun—the car chases, with their practical stunts and heavy synths, are incredible—and the cast is fantastic. Kathleen Turner's inherently Old Hollywood vibe makes her a perfect audience surrogate for this particular story, Danny DeVito is at his put-upon funniest, and Michael Douglas is in rare form, very clearly modeling his Jack Colton after the likes of Han Solo and Snake Plissken. He's always been a cool and compelling screen presence, but I can't think of any other role that allowed him to be such a lovable rogue.

reviews.text: "Run Silent, Run Deep" is a 1958 WWII film directed by Robert Wise. The film specifically takes a look at submarine warfare in the Pacific where Clark Gable is a U.S. Naval officer bent on revenge in taking out a Japanese Destroyer vessel that took out his prior submarine. Since the wreckage in which he narrowly escaped with his life, he has been stuck within an administrative role behind a desk. This hasn't stopped him from recanting the prior events over and over again on paper, something that he has studied and knows that he will surely win if he ever gets a return chance. reviews.author: AndrewC
reviews.text: From Run Silent, Run Deep, you can really see so much of the DNA of subsequent submarine movies that have been made (Crimson Tide being an especially obvious example) and it is itself also a rock-solid war film in its own right. This has all the hallmarks, set-ups, and dialogue of the subgenre and even in its infancy stage, it's all done with lots of tension and excitement squeezed into the fairly short runtime. Having fine actors like Clark Gable and Burt Lancaster also helps in that regard as their commanding performances contribute to Run Silent, Run Deep's status as a terrific blueprint for all submarine war films since its release.

reviews.author: pirateneckbeard
reviews.text: Robert Wise is one of the best versatile directors in the game and is very over looked compared to the auteurs that have been quite honestly over appraised to a certain extent by this reviewer. Any who on to the review. This story is smartly crafted with two solid leads and an armada of character actors with just the right amount of humour to make the poignant scenes sting with humanity. The claustrophobia of the submarine racked up the tension and you see where "Das Boot" got a lot of story elements from. There is so many character dynamics here that don't muddy the waters only enrich the plot. Oh and they did this all in a 90 minute running time!?! This was a lot of fun so glad I immersed myself in this material;)

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Fairly sturdy WWII submarine revenge drama with Clark Gable as the obsessive commander on the hunt for the Japanese destroyer who killed his previous crew and Burt Lancaster as his loyal executive officer who questions the intensely personal fixation of his superior but helps him see it through logistically anyway. Not a lot going on here you haven't seen before in a number of war films and I feel like the sweaty, tortured rage of it isn't as impassioned as it could be in the writing/performances but the FX work is solid and Robert Wise once again effectively shifts styles to suit the subject matter; adhering pretty strictly to the nuts-and-bolts machinery of the mission itself/torpedo strike sequencing in a way that's engaging enough and a clear precursor to a movie like Das Boot.

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: Even though I am a fan of war films, I find it challenging to engage with certain subgenres, particularly those involving submarines, warships, or the air force. I have a preference for films that focus on the battlefields of WWII Europe over the Pacific theatre, and I favour stories of infantrymen in trenches over naval or aviation spectacles. Following recommendations from my LB friends, Rick Burin and Ben (giant13), I decided to watch Robert Wise's Run Silent, Run Deep, which is considered the quintessential Clark Gable film. Despite my reservations about Burt Lancaster, with whom I've had a mixed experience, the fierce determination to upstage each other displayed by both these Hollywood icons truly enhances their performances.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: All you have is your mercy. Sansho the Bailiff is a humanist film of humble scope. It is Mizoguchi operating beyond modernity. It is less a socio-political drama and more a grand historical tale that transcends a critique of any particular moment in time. Sansho the Bailiff is begging only for kindness. Equality is radical, and treating people with love despite their class is something as controversial now as it was in the last century or indeed in any century.

reviews.text: A work of formal perfection (it is its own semester of film studies) in service to maybe the most devastating story I've come across in cinema. This film is so despairing that even water imagery, typically employed to mean a fresh start or a cleansing, is perversely inverted to signal even worse developments. The layered mise-en-scène meshes seamlessly with the acting and narrative, each frame contributing not merely to the mood of the moment but its foundation. One of the greatest films of all time.

reviews.text: Even now, thirty years later, there aren’t many films like SCHOOL DAZE. It’s a big, overstuffed movie, crackling with its director’s obsessions and preoccupations, from the MGM musicals of the 1950s to the politics of the post-civil rights generation of African Americans and the emerging class stratification in black life. It’s heightened, highly-stylized and high energy, with characters that feel simultaneously like archetypes and real, living people.

reviews.text: In the wake of campus protesting in support of Palestine, we are seeing some of the most principled and organized college students since the Vietnam War. It’s heartening to see the students of America stand firmly against genocide and apartheid. The young people of today were born in the waning years of South African apartheid, a historical moment that feels simply too recent to forget. In 1988, Spike Lee made a film about Black students going to a historically Black college with an administration that refused to divest from South Africa. School Daze is a film about the contradictions of modern life, especially for young Black people in America. Lee—who attended Morehouse College as an undergraduate—crafted a thorny, messy film…

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: The storyline is a quite openly a clothesline to hang Jackie Chan action sequences on. Those action sequences rule though; they’re jammed with inventive choreography and whimsical flourishes, and one has Jackie versus Donnie Yen, which is extra fun. I could watch Jackie mess with bumbling bobbies in a revolving door for hours; I could watch him pay homage to Gene Kelly and Harold Lloyd for days. (I also appreciate how Chan and company turned the entire film into an homage to clichéd movies tropes made new again through Chan’s physicality, like the fireplace that spins when you activate the hidden switch, revealing a secret room.)

reviews.text: gimmicky as it can sometimes be i've always found the vision here of holmes as action deconstructionist strangely vivid and compelling if not faithful. it's broadly but quite convincingly woven into the psychology, relationships, politics and of course mechanized digital style. ritchie exuberantly visualizing the constantly shifting sea of layers and machinations with manic kineticism and an industrial aesthetic with the occasional steampunk gesture—this one in particular is a practically lyrical frenzy of small, moving parts where the literal gears of power and history are a collection of man-made tools and motions that contribute to a larger tapestry of huge, almost dreamlike destruction. features some of my favourite POV and slomo camerawork in a major studio movie honestly. anyway as with the other late-ritchie film hardly anybody talked about (Man From U.N.C.L.E.) this is surprisingly great/fun/stylish.

reviews.text: Craven returns to many of his pet themes—the family unit under duress, the illusion of safety by suburban surfaces, a child's escape from repression/abuse/cycle of violent mistakes made by parents, the consumption of violence in media/dreams vs. reality, etc—in this insane mix of teen slasher, serial killer thriller, and sci-fi body-snatching chase movie about a psychic high school football player (played by writer/director extraordinaire Peter Berg) vs. his re-animated serial killer dad. He leans into every ridiculous, gruesome detail of what I imagine he wanted his Nightmare on Elm Street sequels to look like with the confidence of a man working with material far tighter than what he's got here. reviews.text: Wine is probably the most boring subject on Earth, so how come Payne’s film about a lonely, bitter best man (Paul Giamatti) taking the soon-to-be-groom (Thomas Haden Church) on a week-long tour of vineyards is so bloody good? Perhaps because of Giamatti’s astonishing characterisation, which imbues an arrogant, self-destructive, self-hating pseud with a completely disarming humanity. Or perhaps because it’s not really about wine at all, but love and friendship and the choices that people make that end up deciding and defining their lives. It’s the antithesis of formula filmmaking: incredibly entertaining, but also about something, and featuring – quite unexpectedly – a handful of brilliant sight gags.

reviews.text: As great as this movie is, as great as Daniel Craig is, as hard as it is to imagine any other Bond in this movie, it would have been even better and more meaningful if he'd made it when he was 54 instead of 44, or if it was his last Bond instead of his third (out of at least four). The whole script, about Bond's continuing (or perhaps declining) relevance in the modern world, only really makes sense on a metatextual level, because Craig's Bond is still quite clearly an ass kicker of the highest order. If he was the age of, say, Roger Moore circa A VIEW TO A KILL, this movie would have an whole extra layer to it.

reviews.author: PTAbro
reviews.text: Kurt Vonnegut himself remarked that George Roy Hill's adaptation of Slaughterhouse-Five was a "flawless translation." I'd pretty much agree - and that's why this is one of the better examples of how some stories are better suited to the written word. There is a depth of emotion and energy in Vonnegut's novel that somehow does not translate to the film. The deep, dark, manic black humor in his words and sentences does its best to wind its way onto the screen, and I have come to settle on the fact that it's just impossible to duplicate Vonnegut's wit outside of pieces of dialogue and the overarching plot.

reviews.text: Political action thriller from New Zealand about a man who, after splitting from his wife, seeks solitude on a little island in Coromandel. His peace is shattered when he somehow ends up getting dragged into a revolution. Well, no man is an island I guess. The film is based on the book Smith's Dream and presumably has something to say about the political climate in New Zealand at the time (I can't comment as I wasn't there). The story is still of interest - seemingly the main character can't escape from politics even if he pays no attention to it and actually hides away on an island. How depressing! It's the first starring role for Sam Neill and he's one…

reviews.author: ♠ Ben ♠
reviews.text: Both Donaldson and Neill debut in "Sleeping Dogs", a great kiwi political thriller about a family man that, looking for a different life, gets tangled in a revolution. I guess the film could be regarded as a milestone of kiwi cinema considering it was the first New Zealand produced film to gain general release in the US and placed kiwi films in the spotlight, a modest one but still. Sam Neill has always ruled, and here's no exception, he kills it in his debut. The humble budget is evident, but that doesn't keep it from having excellent cinematography, several strong action sequences, and a well-rounded film overall.

reviews.text: Stuart Gordon's Eyes Wide Shut. A wonderfully bizarre, unnatural parody of cutthroat social-climbing Beverly Hills, 90210-esque rich yuppie teenagers coming of age (starring Baywatch actor Billy Warlock as B-movie Marty McFly) that in its final reel morphs into a disgustingly tangible, conspiratorial body horror film where wealth serves as both a superficial cover and conduit for all the psychosexual, Lovecraftian perversities you're told are definitely not happening beneath the surface of power. The utterly repulsive, phantasmagoric goop-incest-orgy finale of this is as surreal and visceral a depiction of class violence and sexual depravity as there's perhaps ever been (shoutout to gore make-up FX legend Screaming Mad George), and feels particularly apt in the midst of the Jeffrey Epstein news. Time to pee in the tea and get shunting. "I'm not paranoid, all my fears are real."

reviews.text: Tarkovsky's failure. Solaris does not transcend genre as Tarkovsky wanted. It is not about faith and the unexplainable. It is about humans, and human creations are the essence of science fiction. Tarkovsky made films in conjunction with God. This is his atheist movie. It is a film of men who discover wonders, but wonders they can travel to, and explain away with their talk of science, and even destroy with their knowledge. Tarkovsky made films about people travelling through worlds that the audience cannot comprehend, except this one time. This is a film of science, not faith.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: The cap of a loose triptych of films about the abasement of American imperial pride in its own backwaters. The first, John Boorman's Deliverance, explicitly emasculated its macho adventurers in a brutal attack on personal and national self-identity. The second, First Blood, found authoritarian confidence so rattled that domestic cops took out their own frustrated sense of control on a rattled, neglected veteran. Southern Comfort sends a National Guard on maneuvers in the Louisiana bayou where they immediately act like invaders, stealing boats from local Cajuns, then being enraged when those people dare to defend their property.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Hill has long been a vocal admirer of the old-school tough and economically-minded Hollywood action directors of the 1930-1950s, and the stripped-down purity of their genre craftsmanship. He always felt he would've been a more fitting contemporary among Hawks, Ford, Boetticher, Walsh, Siegal, Fuller, etc. rather than the New Hollywood revisionists he came up alongside. But similarly to Sam Peckinpah (an artist Hill briefly worked with and blatantly pulled many aesthetic techniques from, especially his love of goopy slomo squibs), he ultimately did find a way to translate the modern 60s-70s ugliness and cruelty onto the old macho formulas he loved, and Southern Comfort might just be his finest example of doing so. Taking the old army patrol mission ensemble…

reviews.author: Todd Gaines
reviews.text: It's Predator without Predators and Aliens without Aliens in Walter Hill's tale of trouble on the bayou. Target practice. Cold fish. Row, Row, Your fuckin' boat. Dead Coyote. Nauls before he met Mac. The way Powers Boothe holds a knife. Bill's biological brother. Casper the reluctant leader. Brion fuckin' James's beard. War paint. DYNO-mite! Stuckey's gold tooth. Kinda-friendly doggies. The ultra-intensity of Fred fuckin' Ward. Louisiana water torture. Grave diggin'. Timber! Blanks make the best cover fire. Quicksand. Firing squad. Swingin' Bubba. Hitchhiking. Wild and crazy Cajun partying. Billy motherfuckin' Sole's mustache. A big-ass piggy. Dancin' straight outta You Got Served. Stabbin' dick. Bayonet. The fuckin' cavalry. A fuckin' intense film that surprisingly doesn't have a shit-ton of action. Fantastic character development with memorable performances from Powers Boothe and Keith Carradine. Moody bluesy soulful music throughout that sets the mood just right. A damn fine war film that you should check out.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Macho paranoid hysteria has rarely been put on-screen with such skill. The knot get tied carefully more and more until those beautiful sustained final 15 minutes at the community. Great ensemble acting and Hill does such a great job of playing around the idea of a fractured group, like the next year’s The Thing (TK Carter is in both), it is the work of a self-appointed Hawks disciple set into twisting a lot of his principles around. The Cajuns hunting the main characters are masters in psychological warfare, they seem less interested into punishing them by killing than making sure every man drawn into their own paranoid madness, the overcompensating wounded male behavior that remains in the background pushed to the breaking point.

reviews.author: Tim Fehrenbach
reviews.text: “i’m not supposed to be here.”Somewhere in all this, there is a kind of comfort, a special kind. Firmly grounded in Southern Gothic, Walter Hill pulls us somewhere between Deliverance and something even meaner – a dense, swampy survival descent that feels weirdly singular. It looks absolutely gorgeous, it’s tense as hell, and it sneaks in more commentary than you’d expect, balancing inner collapse with sharp, nasty flashes of violence that really hit. It plays like an action thriller, bleeding into isolationist folk horror, where landscape and the people themselves form a closed world the soldiers don’t belong to. Ry Cooder’s slide guitar score drizzles along, almost mischievously lulling you in while everything keeps slipping out of control.

reviews.text: Korine updates stylistic elements of Malick and Mann for a vulgar, excessive 2012 online youth party culture American Dream and ends up with one of the greatest accomplishments of his career and the decade: a candy-colored, electronic, alcohol-soaked neo-noir about dissatisfied college girls who in their pursuit of MTV fantasy self-actualization/liberation accidentally come face-to-face with the American class and race realities these fantasies were born from and end up mistresses in a Florida rapper drug war. reviews.text: I’m a bit over the moon here, as it’s not often when one of your favourite films is displaced. In this case, Tarkovsky’s own Solaris. I absolutely adored Solaris for its humanistic take on the hard Sci-Fi nugget of illusion and projection. While I haven’t seen the interceding Mirror, which I’ve seen here has lots of love, it almost seems like Stalker is a follow up fuck-you to Stanley Kubrick. Solaris had a humanistic take on great sci-fi questions, although it was less grand is scope compared to Kubrick’s masterpiece. Here, Tarkovsky matches Kubrick in grand scope and interpretation.

reviews.text: “you think in such three-dimensional terms.”If I put all nostalgia aside – and that’s not an easy thing to do with my favorite of the early installments of this franchise – this might be the best written, most accomplished Star Trek movie. It’s layered, mature, and astonishingly cohesive given everything it’s balancing. It shifts from the Borg’s invasion of the Enterprise – where Picard’s trauma and thirst for revenge blur into the larger fight for control – to the Queen’s eerie seduction of Data and the questions it stirs about temptation and identity. And somehow, it weaves in the near-slapstick absurdity on Earth, and it still works. That it holds together, that these tones resonate instead of clashing, is…

Before you know it, the Borg is attacking Earth, the crew is disobeying Star Fleet command, but even that's all prelude to being thrown back in time, where the Borg are attempting to rewrite First Contact. This is the ST:TNG movie we were waiting for. Each member of the regular cast get a chance to shine.

And even then, I'm not sure how well it would play to a Trek newbie, since so much of its power and themes come from Kirk and Spock being older, and the ways that time has changed them both. Middle age is a nightmare for Kirk. His body is betraying him (the dreaded reading glasses), and he takes no pleasure in the rank of an admiral if a starship doesn't come with it. (His itchiness to return to action was one of the smarter things that Star Trek: The Motion Picture did.)…

reviews.text: I hate this movie for all its cutesy quoting of Wrath of Khan while trying and spectacularly failing to sublet its gravitas. I hate it for casting the whitest actor on Earth as a man named Khan Noonien Singh. I hate it for the way that every shot in the back half is a three-ring circus of lens flares, cluttered sets, and CGI embellishments. I hate it for turning Spock into Sheldon from "The Big Bang Theory". I hate it for its abuse of Leonard Nimoy's fealty to the franchise and to J.J. Abrams, reducing Old Spock to a fortune-teller Young Spock now keeps on speed dial. I hate this movie, this hacky, weightless, soulless "Muppet Babies" theme-episode of a movie.

reviews.author: Kristen S. Hé 何盛皓
reviews.text: François Truffaut once said, “It is impossible to make a true anti-war film, because the act of looking at violence is inherently exciting”. Robert A. Heinlein wrote, “Violence, naked force, has settled more issues in history than has any other factor”. Paul Verhoeven’s Starship Troopers would have had them both rolling in their graves. Verhoeven’s 1997 adaptation throws good taste — and Heinlein’s original novel — out the window. The rare film that indulges the horrors of war and the joys of watching it vicariously, Starship Troopers makes the wrong feel so appealing because, quite simply, it is.

reviews.text: I find it fascinating how time naturally reevaluates the importance of certain genres, styles, and art. Robert Mitchum once stated noir as, "we just called 'em B-movies" and sure enough, the era is now exclusively remembered for them. We're kind of going through a renaissance of that ourselves, what was once seen as low-brow eighties trash is accepted with grimy hands and open beers to a generation that grew up loving them fondly now dusted off from their hippocampus libraries. What we remember is not necessarily what was the most popular, but what was the most impactful. This insurgency of anachronisms. In a roundabout way, because that's how I'm doing it with this review, that brings us to Stormy Monday!…

reviews.text: Mike Figgis' written and directed neo-noir thriller Stormy Monday manages to strike a particular mood as it follows Irishman Brendan (Sean Bean), a janitor for a club and waitress/prostitute Kate (Melanie Griffith). Set in Newcastle, the film is primarily carried by its small, secondary elements, with Figgis' almost perfectly regulating maintenance of its tone as it blends scenes and stories with unemphatic assurance. It begins not unlike a Robert Altman movie, with the delights laying within its grasp of characters and some subtle scene-stealing moments with its supporting actors, including Sting and Tommy Lee Jones. However, it's not as thematically profound as Altman, nor does it scratch as deeply, preferring to stay in a lower key and much smaller scale.…

reviews.author: Maria
reviews.text: There is great tragedy in Superman Returns. After five years of searching for his home planet, Superman returns on Earth to find a world that doesn’t need him anymore. Mankind has survived without a savior, and Lois Lane has moved on from their undefined relationship; now, she has a son and is engaged. More than fighting against evil, he must fight to regain the trust of those he once knew and who have admired him. But it isn’t an easy battle. The two sides of him that should be be in complete harmony are severed from each other, and with every success that comes Superman’s way, Clark Kent is buried further and further into obscurity.

reviews.text: Based on several adventures of the wildly popular Italian comic book character Tex Willer, Tex and the Lord of the Deep was simultaneously an attempt to revive the spaghetti western and a pilot for a hoped-for RAI TV series about the character. Published for the first time in 1948, the Tex series was the most successful comic in Italian history, and its title character — a man of uncompromising principles who was both a Texas Ranger and a friend to indigenous people (at one point in the series, he becomes chief of all the Navajo) — was a beloved figure, not just in Italy but also around the world (the series' following in Brazil is, reportedly, particularly big).

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: Giuliano Gemma once again reunites with the director responsible for his A Pistol for Ringo (1965) star turn, Duccio Tessari, to tackle the immensely popular Bonelli/Gallepini western comic, Tex. Tessari's earlier peplum scripts usually incorporated fantastical elements, so the weird west is in full effect as Tex tackles a mummification dart shooting Aztec cult. Gemma will be aided by William Berger as Kit Carson. More adventure than western, Tex comes across as a tribute to serials - not unlike Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981), but lacks the big set pieces or creative flourishes to do right by its source material. The end result is less Indiana Jones and more in the vein of SCTV's Six Gun Justice.

reviews.text: This looks fantastic, too bad there's no really good transfer of it out there. McTiernan remains a master of spatial clarity even in pitch darkness or in pea-soup fog, although not in the way you might think. His characters are as disoriented as we are but firelight and silhouette are constantly used as landmarks, not locating us inside a space but opening or closing the immediate space around us. Famously this was taken away from him but much like Woo with MISSION: IMPOSSIBLE 2 the eye here is a singular one even if the scissors belonged to someone else. Bit of a shame this isn't closer to the "Forensic Beowulf" of Crichton's novel but that's neither here nor there.

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: Almost painful because you can tell there's a 5-star film in here somewhere, if only control hadn't been wrested from John MicTiernan—"The 13th Warrior" feels clearly compromised (the final battle lasts all of five minutes and I don't think there's a single shot of Antonio Banderas fighting during it!), but the hacked runtime does mean this thing moves fast, mercilessly fast, and there's still so much here I enjoy. The major sequences are simply awash in atmosphere: the dense fog, flaming torches, and heads cleaved clean off their bodies, it's like a portrait of hell in motion. Hadn't seen this since it was new on VHS(!) and it's aged far better than I would have expected; you can definitely see traces of DNA for Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" trilogy and "Game of Thrones" here. McTiernan was one of the greats.

But was the film really that bad, or was it simply a case of the inflated budget and some poor initial reviews scuppering any chance it had? Based loosely on the Michael Crichton novel Eaters Of The Dead, with a few nods in the direction of some Norse legends, this historical action film does have some fine moments of battlefield carnage. Brutal and bloody, but with the odd comic touch thrown into the mix, this sees Arab poet (?) Antonio Banderas accompany Norsemen…

reviews.author: Deckk
reviews.text: 100-word review: The 13th Warrior is somewhat shallow work of historical fiction that prioritises spectacle over substance. The film is primarily concerned with battle scenes, which are well-staged but dominate the screen time, leaving little room for character development, making it hard for viewers to care about the outcome of said battles. The supporting cast of Viking warriors is largely indistinguishable from one another, and Ibn Fahdlan's transformation from outsider to warrior feels rushed and under explored. The story lacks depth, with much of the plot driven by a series of encounters with a shadowy enemy rather than a compelling narrative arc.

I couldn't believe that these people were tricked by Oppenheimer until I realized, actually they know exactly what's going on. They understand they are to be filmed reminiscing upon choking people, stabbing people, beheading people, and much, much worse, and they are happy to share this with the rest of the world because to them they are right…

reviews.text: Much to say about the beautiful sets, gorgeous cinematography and restrained (for Scorsese) camera work. But on this first watch, I am especially struck by how expressive the three leads are within the rigid confines of the Victorian mores they are performing. Lewis’ aching desire, Pfeiffer’s deep frustration and Ryder’s deceptive innocence are all so clearly conveyed even as they are communicated by the slightest of looks, of glances, of movements. Brilliant work all around.
