reviews.author: King #adoptdontshop
reviews.text: Flashy, quick and throws lots of surprises along the way, The Bank Job is not your usual heist film. This Jason Statham-led action thriller is shaped around a manipulative plot that fascinates and excites, even though the pre-heist preparation arc is something viewers probably watched in a dozen other films. The Bank Job banked on its strong characters acted by a willful cast (Saffron Burrows is so beautiful argh), quick pacing, witty dialogue, justifiable emotional touches, and crafty storytelling - resulting in an above average action entertainment from start to finish. And the advertised “based on real events” slogan umps the intrigue (will Google the story right after).

reviews.author: AndrewC
reviews.text: Colour me surprised, The Bank Job is actually a pretty tasty British heist thriller that sees Jason Statham in a different sort of role than you normally expect from him. He's less the usual action hero he plays this time, and the movie overall is a fairly traditional heist film more interested in suspense and dialogue than shootouts, punch-ups, or chases. Statham fits into it well and he's backed by a fine supporting roster that play their parts convincingly. It's all guided with skill by an old pro like Roger Donaldson and even with its historical inaccuracies and struggles to weave together all the plot strands, The Bank Job is solid stuff through and through.

reviews.text: This movie is simply obsessed with squishing people’s eyeballs out of their heads like a Panic Pete stress toy. Lucio Fulci was horrified by the human body, which he depicts here as a wet, mostly hollow container of tendons made of chewing gum and packed with almost magenta blood that shoots out of you like a t-shirt cannon if you so much as scratch yourself. The gore is beautiful and Fulci presents it to you like a cat bringing you a mole. Gruesome but almost sweet. But by the tenth mole you begin to have some questions about the situation with your yard.

reviews.text: The most genuinely chilling film ever made, not just because of its ideas, but because of how intricately and sophisticated the film is at translating them. And then twice as chilling, because this is what establishes the primary functions of narrative cinema. A really challenging film to write about - virtually impossible to write about this cohesively within capsule format, so here are just some notes - a proper study of the film would require an entire book.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Perhaps the ugliest film I've ever seen, but also one of the most essential in terms of establishing the language of cinema. Griffith's astonishing photography and montage that would later define a lot of the cinematic vocabulary still used today serves only as a temporary distraction from horrid, overbearing racism; his use of close-ups and cross-cutting, in particular, is just so far beyond what anyone else was doing at the time, and many of the Hollywood legends who would employ them in the years to come worked on one of his sets and learned it from him, so it's hard to a imagine a world where he and this film don’t exist or get taught in film history classes. But as much as I appreciate its formal innovation and place in cinematic history there is just no way to separate it from the evil being communicated here on a narrative or thematic level.

reviews.text: A truly deadened-soul work defined by its stark, virulent anti-blackness. But my big problem lately is that this shit is still taught in undergrad and grad programs under the guise of D.W. Griffith having “innovated” cinema. To this day, I see people who should know better crediting Griffith with everything from the creation of the close-up to cross-cutting. Which is a lie Griffith successfully propagated. There are examples in silent cinema of such techniques before this egregious film came on the scene. Alongside Native Americans, black people are the only people routinely asked to put aside the fact that films like this ask for the brutalization and extinction of our people in order to marvel at the technical innovations and aesthetic worth that isn’t even fucking there.

reviews.text: Think Mad Max meets Mystery, Alaska sounds like an oddly intriguing mash-up? Then you’ll likely dig this blood-spattered feel-good movie. The Blood of Heroes follows a marauding band of professional Juggers as they roam the barren Australian Outback trying to make a buck. (Jugger is a fictionalized sport that is difficult to define; imagine if field hockey was alloyed with elements of medieval/gladiatorial warfare — the two forged & wrought together with dog skulls, battle axes, spiked spears/clubs, swirling chains, and makeshift equipment. It’s definitely a team game, but often resembles a bludgeoning free-for-all of competitive carnage.)

reviews.author: LateNightFrames
reviews.text: Also known as Salute of the Jugger, this one builds a strange, fully realized world around a brutal traveling sport. It’s scrappy and low-budget, but the commitment to its setting gives it a unique identity. The action is rough and physical, lacking polish but full of impact. There’s a mythic, almost folklore-like quality to how the story unfolds. Weird, gritty, and more memorable than it first appears.

reviews.author: Neill Shaughness
reviews.text: Honestly this is much more enjoyable than I would have guessed. Like most examples of the 80s post apocalyptic genre, this film's production design clearly strains against its budget, forcing it to have much of the same "Mad Max light" quality the genre became known for. This is a shame too, because the script is not half bad for a cheap dystopian sci fi. The stakes are much more personal than they usually are in this genre, the fictional sport at the center of the movie is better conceived than most, allowing the sports genre elements to actually work, and the cast is pretty damn solid too. Yes it's cheesy and yes it's predictable, but it's also a fun time if you accept the movie on its own terms.

Even if I'm wrong about this being the superior entry, these films remain miracles of 2nd unit work and editing, somehow dealing out coherent sequences from all that sloppy handheld coverage, cutting ahead of movement instead of on it (although I think they fail consistently in that they cut away from individual impacts, a pet peeve of mine), and it can't really be overstated how much this benefited from the shock of the new. Dan Bradley gets none of the credit frequently attributed to Greengrass, all the more a shame since QUANTUM OF SOLACE remains the best example of this style, sadly despised simply because it's off-brand for Bond.

All the same, good to know where "A Few Good Men" knicked some of its own techniques (the famous Nicholson blow-out climax originated here with Bogart, for one). Most of this movie though is a fictitious hypothetical "Mutiny on the Bounty" showing why a group of Navy officers gradually turn against captain Bogart. That man is just a joy to watch.

He's a mama's boy — never an attractive attribute in a protagonist — and he's involved with the most milquetoast cabaret performer to ever grace a Hollywood picture. Even by 50s standards this romance is dullsville. By the time we're an hour into this, you can't imagine what the seven Oscar nominations and the film's reputation among film fans are all about.…

reviews.author: Christian Ha
reviews.text: The Colony appears decent at first glance but completely falls short overall. It's a formulaic and unoriginal mess of a post-apocalyptic movie, offering nothing new or compelling. The characters failed to engage me, and I felt indifferent towards their fates. While the action scenes were passable, they still felt somewhat absurd. Despite some goofy moments, the film's overall tone is excessively bleak. Ultimately, it's a forgettable and derivative zombie movie that I only watched in the hopes it might redeem itself as a decent entry in the genre. This movie isn't even remotely passable, and I strongly advise against watching it. Learn from my mistake and steer clear.

reviews.text: A decent attempt, but in the end another reminder that Americans struggle to be truly cynical/realistic about how political power is exercised in their country. They try for hard edged realism, but that gooey patriotic optimism is always just below the surface of even those who proclaim themselves as possessing the toughest of hides. It's no surprise that two of the most successful skewerings of US politics of late have been Veep and House of Cards, both of which are British imports. In the UK the default position is that politicians are automatically suspect, and there is no romanticising of parliament and prime ministers in the way so many Americans still gush over Washington and the White House. reviews.text: Healing comes from nature, and from within, in the wake of sacrifice and assault, in the wake of fundamental shifts in the world. The first time, it is an eerie raid of a lively party, in the relics of ancient genocide. The second time, the survivors bask in crystal-reflected light, after both willingly offered to give up something important for something more important. One offered life for the world, the other the world for life. They achieve symmetry in this moment, and the consequences are further symmetry, light through the crystal, fragmented but perfectly shaped. Life and death are intertwined here.

reviews.text: I love snowy western, I love revenge thrillers, and I love the Alps, so a movie that combines all three is right up my alley. “The Dark Valley” pleasantly surprised me. The actual plot might not be that innovative or surprising, but the film oozes style and atmosphere. It´s bleak, tense, and gripping, with a strong sense of foreboding and a brutally violent climax that pays off the slow-burn buildup. Andreas Prochaska directs the hell out of this film, the standout aspects being the superb cinematography, chilling score, and stunning Austrian mountain setting. I also have to praise the strong performances, first and foremost Sam Riley, who is a great embodiment of the “stoic loner with a mysterious past” archetype.…

Boorman’s choice to have the majority of the film take place inside the “jungle”—rather than the white man/John Wayne’s “garden”—is an audacious, bold swing for a white filmmaker, and it positions the film within a post-colonial framework. In contrast to The Searchers, the depiction of child-snatching indigenous peoples is, for the most part, an admirable attempt at respect (I think). reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: German shock genre cinema's mistrust of the culture's supposed rejection of its fascist history is an essential motivator (see also NEKROMANTIK for example). It's easy to focus on the simple fact of this young girl's ultimately violent obsession with a pop star but it's more about her discovery that the object of her desire is just as integrated into the adult patriarchal world that she hopes to flee with her fantasy. One entrenched system of control (parents, teachers, police, media) hasn't been removed or substituted but simply re-skinned, made more insidiously attractive. Maybe the only course of action is to consume it as completely as it has consumed us, to hybridize. Or is that another trap? Insane soundtrack on this too.

reviews.author: Scumbalina
reviews.text: How have I never reviewed this? I must have seen it four or five times now. Watched at the New Bev, it looked beautiful in 35mm although I prefer the original language track to the english dub. So much of what sells this film is the intense almost silent performance from Desiree Nosbusch. There's so much subtle longing in her face that she really takes you on the journey. Time stands still in this fantasy she's built and you see her float further and further from reality. I've felt a lot of things while watching Der Fan, least of all is sympathy for "R". Despite the insanity of Simone's behavior, you're always somehow with her emotionally. Eckhart Schmidt captures this descent so beautifully that I may as well be watching a nature tape. Her passion has a texture and a taste, something coppery with grit. It's cold and blue, and amidst her devastation is some kind of psycho meditation.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: Of the two films made in the last half decade about internet-based social evolution/revolution, it is a sad statement about current zeitgeist that the film regarding the social network was more solidly made and much better received than the film about exposing corruption in world governments. It is easy to see what "The Fifth Estate," the film about WikiLeaks founder, Julian Assange, is trying to do. Like "The Social Network," it wants to be a slick expose on a man and his pioneering creation. Unlike Fincher's film, "The Fifth Estate" can not muster the narrative balance and interesting characters to cement it as a better-than-above average experience.

reviews.author: Nuttycrazypaws
reviews.text: Forewarning: Real rats were likely harmed in the production of The Food Of The Gods. At least this goofy ecothriller makes effective use of its Pacific Northwest setting. The oppressive grays amid muted yet lush earth tones almost make you forget the unsimulated rodent peril. A veteran of creature features like Gordon seems to have a better eye for visuals than his contemporaries. Or maybe giant rats appeal to me more than the giant bunnies from Night Of The Lepus. The variety of low-budget special effects are never convincing but always fascinating. Too bad the script zigzags between a few too many Romeroesque subplots (football dreams, capitalist ethics, pregnancy fears, et cetera). Despite the quickie epilogue, the human element is too thin for the wider threat posed by rampant growth to feel earned. Gortner has the same reptilian charm as Steve Railsback.

The film depicts this mysterious bubbling “food” source from the ground that a nearby farm in British Columbia had its chickens eat and mutated their offspring into larger-than-man monsters, unaware that a rodent population had been feeding on this substance too. reviews.text: "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo" is a tense and gripping thriller that, in my opinion, slightly surpasses Fincher's remake. Maybe it's the colder, more realistic atmosphere, but this version left a stronger impression on me. The story starts off relatively simple: a disgraced journalist and a brilliant but troubled hacker team up to investigate an old missing person case. But as the film progresses, the mystery deepens, turning into something far darker, filled with family secrets, hidden truths, and disturbing violence. The film doesn’t shy away from difficult topics like abuse, misogyny, and the corrupting power of certain social dynamics. The acting is flawless, every actor brings their character to life with great authenticity. The direction doesn’t rely on flashy effects but focuses on substance, and it works perfectly. It’s a raw, intelligent, and compelling movie, in my opinion it's one of the best thrillers of the last 20 years.

reviews.text: Phillip Pullman’s His Dark Materials series are not the easiest novels to adapt from. Although their main character is a young girl the themes, events and structure of the novels are more suitable for adults. Chris Weitz’s The Golden Compass makes lots of mistakes in its adaptation and the worst of them is that its narrative style and its depiction of the novel is more childish than the original books. The movie is visually convincing but it doesn’t have an idea what to do with Pullman’s elaborate and somehow confusing novel. Characters are one dimensional, their motivations are not clear, none of them are exciting and the main character is so clichéd and predictable that the audience loses interest in her fate. This movie was met with such criticism and had such a bad box office performance that the producers decided to abandon the franchise. That was a right decision. His Dark Materials deserves better than this.

reviews.text: The Gorgon is among the most melancholy of Hammer supernatural films, full of hopelessness, desperation for connection, and men pretending to have control. There is a profound joylessness to the tale, from the opening vignette in which a pregnancy becomes a burden and a sign of failure, to the closing, in which we finally get a glimpse of the title character's eyes, which are red as if she has been crying for the centuries since the death of her sisters (and weeping for every death she causes). No one is happy, and the glimpses of a future in which the sun comes out are so fleeting as to cause those who have them even greater pain when they realize life…

reviews.text: A dark-hearted neonoir comes to a boil under the bright Los Angeles sun, in British director Stephen Frears’s rousing adaptation of the novel by dime-store bard Jim Thompson, a film that raises pulp to the realm of existential tragedy. A possessive mother (Anjelica Huston), her cynical son (John Cusack), and his scheming, seductive girlfriend (Annette Bening) are career swindlers circling one another in an elaborate emotional confidence game that grows increasingly perverse as love and trust turn to betrayal and Oedipal undercurrents rise to the surface. In Frears’s first film made in Hollywood, the ever-assured director and his trifecta of magnetic actors conjure a moody, unstuck-in-time vision of toxic Americana.

reviews.text: More a note than a review: I have a new theory about this movie. When I saw it initially at the theatre, I didn't have quite the same off-kilter hall-of-nowhere experience I had had watching Ju-On: The Grudge and so was faintly disappointed but not too badly. The Shirley Jackson story is one of my favorites, and this is truly a fitting rendering of it. The skeptical approach allows for you to see what you want: a haunted woman or a gaslit woman. Either way, it resonates.

reviews.author: Brian Tallerico
reviews.text: An elegy for the end of an era that feels more mournful because of how much Lee refuses to mock these characters for their flaws, embracing their insecurities instead. The tragedy of the final act resonates so much more than the average suburbanites-behaving-badly genre entry because we can feel the sadness throughout the film. And his work with ensemble was arguably never better. Everyone here strikes just the right chord. It's a great film.

reviews.author: Auteur
reviews.text: Ang Lee is simply one of the greatest directors alive. Last year's Life Of Pi solidified that for me. I would compare him to Stanley Kubrick in the way he is able to adapt to many different genres, and master them. Examining any three of his films in a row, in this case 1997's The Ice Storm, an atmospheric, fatalist drama of 1970's New England suburbanite family dysfunction, sandwiched between 1995's Jane Austen period comedy Sense And Sensibility, and 1999's civil war drama Ride With The Devil, shows an artist unwilling to settle into a comfort zone.

reviews.author: Catherine Stebbins
reviews.text: there is something so sad & pathetic about the adults in The Ice Storm. their disconnect & isolation, esp in the adults. kevin kline having an affair with the sexy neighbor? of course he is! but she bores of him & *flees from her own house*, leaving him to sit around in his boxers. joan allen's frigid wife starts stealing? of course she does! and is immediately caught! these people are so miserably ill-equipped to even function, let alone flourish, within the cliches they have become. not sure how this worked when it came out, or how it still does through 20+ years of white suburbia in crisis movies & period pieces like Mad Men (diff era i know). but it's top-tier. actors at the top of their game playing lost & isolated characters. that final scene is gutting. the unresolved silence & quiet sobs of the final scene. nobody communicates. as kline's ben says, they are always "on the verge".

reviews.text: Without an ounce of hyperbole, I am telling you that Tom Hooper is one of the very worst directors to ever attain "professional" status. This is a nightmarish visual experience. The wanton violations of the 180-degree rule. The bizarre compositions in which characters are pointlessly consigned the extreme right or left of the frame with acres of dead space next to them. The way his camera will arbitrarily shift into Terry Gilliam-vision. His inability to consider what the impact of a space should be, and how to correctly communicate that idea visually. People rightly give Kevin Smith a hard time for his visual illiteracy, but Tom Hooper is so much worse.

reviews.text: As deeply disturbing, relevant, and beautiful in 35mm as ever. Ariel Schudson's excellent piece on The Knack gives a lot of important insight into Lester's complex commentary on the historical oppression of women by a heterosexual patriarchy gone bonkers with the idea of "the knack." The key cutaway gag — which, typical with Lester, happens so fast your mind barely has time to register it, but it's there, folks — is one involving Colin's class of boys, being spoon-fed lines to parrot back like "A man must learn to develop the knack."

reviews.text: Well, maybe sometimes a movie is just too perfectly suited to its particular time and place to have a long shelf life. Richard Lester’s freewheeling, Palme d’Or winning comedy The Knack... and How to Get It might be such a film. As a time capsule of Swinging London, with all its Mods and Rockers and their sexual revolution being observed by stuffy disapproving elders, it’s still an interesting watch. As an enjoyable comedy viewed in the year 2020, I found it slightly exhausting.

reviews.text: Well, I have to say, that was disappointing. Disappointing for two reasons: the book being a masterclass in suspense and Alfred Hitchcock being considered the "Master of Suspense". And bearing that in mind, I believe that creating expectations for a film adaptation in his hands, wasn't entirely my fault. Especially since my experience with "Psycho" a long time ago, I remember finding it a masterclass in filmmaking. But while one holds this title for me, The Lady Vanishes is a masterclass in resilience, in how not to give up halfway through and go all the way to the end. Even if it's unaffectedly boring.

reviews.text: One of the more unfairly maligned American films of the 21st century, and among the small handful of genuine anomalies within Disney’s 2010s lineup that mostly consisted of assembly line filmmaking. Lovingly crafted with so much passion from everyone involved, wholly succeeding both as a throwback to classical westerns and also being a condemnation of capitalism/a deconstruction of Old West myths. Fantastically directed, carefully written, and terrifically performed, with Armie Hammer in particular delivering what remains by and far the best performance of his career.

reviews.text: Really solid, lowkey paperback neo-noir from Scott Frank (hot off two Elmore Leonard adaptations) that's really smart to keep its character detail and heist elements very low-level/intimate/local, etc while slowly ratcheting up its slick suspense thrills into something that feels bigger. Only real misstep here for me is how little room it leaves for its criminals to get pathetic and farcical and nasty when things start going wrong and instead expects you to get very seriously involved in its broadly calculated sentimentality. reviews.author: Danny
reviews.text: “The Making of Superman III” provides an intriguing glimpse into the 1983 film’s production, marked by its bold shift to a comedic tone under Richard Lester’s direction. It explores the choice to spotlight Richard Pryor’s quirky Gus Gorman, a departure from the epic stakes of prior films, alongside Christopher Reeve’s still-captivating Superman. The documentary delves into the innovative yet divisive split-personality Clark vs. Superman sequence and the challenges of blending slapstick with superheroics. While acknowledging the film’s mixed reception, it celebrates the creative risks and technical achievements. Engaging anecdotes and archival clips make it a worthwhile watch for fans curious about this quirky sequel’s creation.

This changes the question, the unproven claim is not challenged and instead the conversation focuses on ‘how many are there?’

reviews.text: The Medallion is an action comedy fantasy about a medallion that gives superhuman abilities. This Gordon Chan movie gets unfavorable marks for being more goofball than kung fu outing. Jackie Chan's usually winning charismatic charms and his fine chemistry with Lee Evans on supporting duty gave The Medallion a little ray of hope, but the overall execution is, to put it plainly, terrible! From the tedious storytelling and skewed transitions to uncoordinated fight choreography and lame scripting, Jackie's fans would feel blindsided by this cartoonish experience. Kids may like this (or not?) but I wish there was more focus here. Overall, The Medallion is so butchered it won’t get any laureate or medals for such a disposable output.

Teaming Jackie Chan up with Tucker from There's Something About Mary probably sounded inspired at the time but it just comes off a little weird. The action is a watered down Chan experience with Jackie looking older and moving a little slower, and more cuts and close-ups to try to hide that. The stunt doubles for Claire Forlani and Julian Sands (in Warlock mode, searching for a magic relic) are extremely noticeable and the special effects are laughable. Also, who thought it was a good idea to put the sound of cats meowing over a fight between two women? I intended to double feature this with The Tuxedo but this one killed my desire to immediately watch another movie that looked so similar.

reviews.author: Karsten
reviews.text: Noah Baumbach’s work is like piano music. It takes two points, whether those points be birth and death, love and hate, New York and LA, and examines the in between. It’s comprised of small moments, small notes, each providing a singular mood that, when put together, combines into a larger, more spastic piece. But there’s precision to that. These notes aren’t thrown together at random, one note always goes hand in hand with the next in a melodic way. It’s a series of different notes played from the same piano, each making it obvious through their sound that they come from the same instrument. It’s why when ‘The Meyerowitz Stories’ ends with a piece with strings, you feel the difference. These once singular sounds blend into something grander, something warmer. A newly-found sense of togetherness.

reviews.author: ChrisStuckmann
reviews.text: It’s 1996. I’m eight years old. I’ve just walked out of a showing of The Phantom, wearing my awesome skull ring Paramount provided to all kids who saw the movie. I stare at the poster. I’m confused by the tagline: Slam Evil! Is he slamming evil in the face? How exactly does one slam evil? Over the next few years, I watch the animated Phantom 2040, renting it from Blockbuster dozens of times. I see Titanic or Zoolander and when Billy Zane shows up I think, ‘That’s the Phantom.’ I read Roger Ebert’s 3.5/4 star review and think: ‘Finally someone understands me.’ In 2025, I rewatch the movie and think: ‘Yup. Still rips. Purple tights and all.’

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: Playing true to its yesteryear pulp design, "The Phantom" easily holds up on my return visit to it, this time in a very clean 4k format. While the character flies under the radar compared to staples like Superman and Batman, the character of the Phantom debuted back in 1936, created by Lee Falk and widely considered to be the first "costumed superhero" according to Guinness World Records. Although I somewhat think this factoid is up for debate (as it probably is the "The Golden Bat" who first was created in 1930), the is no doubt the influence of "The Phantom" being the first character dubbed a superhero by the western world and gracing the pages in newspaper serial form.

reviews.text: I’m a sucker for physical comedy, especially of the slapstick variety. And The Pink Panther Strikes Again contains some of my favorite slapstick routines, both from the Pink Panther series and beyond. It also contains Peter Sellers as (now) Chief Inspector Jacques Clouseau, a characterization that never ceases to entertain me. So, I must depart ways with Pauline Kael, who once described Sellers' performance in this film as “joyless” and suggested that “Clouseau’s clenched-jaws politesse is a joke that has run its course”—a sentiment echoed by Roger Ebert that same year. True, we don’t arrive at any new insights into this cartoon of a man. But as far as I can tell, Sellers brings the same energy to this role…

reviews.text: Scene for scene, I think you could make a case for this as one of the funniest movies ever made. It isn't as glossy or tightly structured as the other top-tier Inspector Clouseau film, A Shot in the Dark, but this is the one that never fails to get me howling right from the beginning thanks to the one of the most hilarious opening scenes ever committed to film. How on earth Herbert Lom never earned an honorary Oscar of some kind is beyond me; he's easily as funny as Sellers here, and his comic timing is impeccable as he goes from borderline sane and collected to raving insanity within the span of about five minutes. So many classic scenes here: the parallel bars, "Does your dog bite?," the entire whodunit interrogation scene, storming the castle, the dentist disguise, "Come to Me"... it's all pure gold.

reviews.author: Rizki
reviews.text: Michael Radford's The Postman follows the sweet and engaging friendship between a seemingly dim-witted postman named Mario Ruoppolo (Massimo Troisi) and the famous Chilean poet Pablo Neruda (Philippe Noiret), set on an Italian island near Sicily. I could call the friendship unlikely, but what would have been truly unlikely would have been for Pablo to dismiss a man like Mario. Why would a man who's been exiled from his homeland reject someone like Mario himself? Rejection is the ugly fruit of judgment, and judgment is a perversion of rationality, which is itself estranged from poetry.

reviews.text: if the gauntlet was the platonic ideal of the 70s cop film: a relaxed tone, stark cinematography, featuring a lone man against the system, loaded with practical stunts, then the rookie is the platonic ideal of the 80s/90s cop film: jam-packed full of ridiculous macho quips, a funky score, two contrasting buddy-cops, a huge bodycount, and loads of explosions! i don't know why the hell this isn't talked about more, because it's really fun, never boring, and shot with eastwood's trademark unfussy style. it's almost a parody of what a cop movie is, and relishes in exaggerating every possible cliche. very underrated!

reviews.text: Apparently in order to convince Warner to foot the bill for his more personal and uncommercial passion project White Hunter, Black Heart Clint agreed to do this for-hire script by two young in-house writers who were hired to provide the studio with a buddy cop movie that knowingly hit every big box office trope and trend of the 80s maximalist action-comedy. As a result, there is a bizarre tension and sleepy energy to this derived from the fact that a movie clearly meant for a Shane Black or Tony Scott is starring and being directed by a 60-year-old Eastwood who was clearly eager to leave the Dirty Harry sequels behind him and move on to his more somber, self-reflective run…

Other entries in the series usually have strong women characters, but not here, and there isn’t much humor. Still, the film is mildly diverting, and it’s fun to try to guess the identity of the killer. Dr. Watson’s reference to one of G. K. Chesterton’s Father Brown stories is a clue. It’s a bit odd that why Holmes and Watson are in Canada is never explained, nor is why they are able to cross the Atlantic during WWII.…

reviews.text: Surely one of the best of the Rathbone/Bruce Sherlock Holmes series. The plot riffs on the Hounds of the Baskervilles and follows the dynamic duo a village in Canada, where they investigate the murder of a woman which the locals believe to be the work of a legendary local monster. The whole mystery is very well put together. The story flows briskly and there's always plenty going on. Basil Rathbone and Nigel Bruce have such a great chemistry together; the former providing all the drive and intelligence, and the latter giving amusing comic relief. The atmosphere is great but the best thing about this film is the mystery itself, which really turns the whole whodunit trope on its head in…

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: I always end up with more questions than answers when I watch these Rathbone and Bruce films, with my first one here being, what were Holmes and Watson doing attending an Occult Conference in Canada during WWII? Regardless, the intrepid duo get drawn into yet another murder plot, one that has an age old legend of a monster that prowls the marshes around the village of La Port Rouge, a monster that Holmes instantly dismisses in his own unique way, before piecing together another of those plots that only make sense to savants. We get more awful disguises, more fog and chases through dark marshes, and the wonderful use of a five-pronged garden implement to hide a murderer among folklore. Gerald Hamer and Paul Cavanagh complete the cast here, but four films into this franchise and I'm running out of things to say about both the plots and how to review them properly?

I admit, I wasn't paying attention a lot of the time because them religious horrors, it just doesn't matter to me what ends up happening as there aren't that many variations (God Told Me to being an exception). reviews.author: Servix
reviews.text: For me it was one of those horror films that stirs more curiosity than true connection. We start with a compelling premise revolving around a telepathic young man whose unconscious mind sends vivid emotions and hallucinations into the world around him. Unfortunately, it never quite grabs the way you want it to. You can tell they were after an introspective, art house vibe rather than the slasher stylings of its era, and while that ambition gives the film a distinct tone, it also leaves me feeling distant. The atmosphere is eerie, the visuals stylish, and the concept is definitely cool, but none of it made me fall in love. It’s not bad and certainly not boring, just the kind of film that earns respect more than devotion.

reviews.text: A masterwork of outstanding direction, terrific writing & brilliant acting, a fascinating yet unsettling portrait of poverty, desperation, greed & its corrupting power, and still retaining all its potency despite being nearly 70 years old, The Treasure of the Sierra Madre is one of American cinema's finest works that not only ranks amongst the best films of the 1940s but is one of the greatest movies ever made.

reviews.author: Colin the dude
reviews.text: One small step for man, one giant leap for Hollywood. A landmark turning point in the business, Madre was one of the very first to shoot almost entirely on location, resulting in an unheard of 6 months of shooting. The painstaking details have lived long, gracefully aging this story like the finest wine you've tasted. A classic that time has proven will live forever. Walter Huston's performance only turns your ideas of prospecting wild men completely upside down with spellbinding charm. The roots of Daniel Plainview seed their way back to Huston's face in this.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: What a magnificent, raw, and realistic work about problems so many choose to ignore. An urban narrative stripped of sweetness and euphemism, one that tears apart the romanticized idealizations of a society that refuses to look at its own abandoned children, at the open wounds scattered through the alleys and sidewalks of the city. The work penetrates, without concessions, the marginalized world of youth in poverty, exposing with brutal honesty the failure of the social, familial, and institutional structures that should protect the most vulnerable.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: A pool of helplessness. Los Olvidados does not find virtue or nobility in poverty. It just finds pain. This is a film with no romantic notions, just ruthless characters in unfortunate circumstances. While at times Los Olvidados is reminiscent of the darkest versions of social realism, Luis Buñuel maintains his trademark surrealism. There are odd shots, unexpected imagery, and disturbed dreams. The film uses plenty of implication too, in order to discuss sex and violence within the limits of the time. The grisly deaths are not always believable but they are strongly felt in their harshness. Los Olvidados presents a world of destitute children, struggling mothers, and disabled men living in poverty. There is no logic to Los Olvidados, just…

It follows a group of kids as they cause trouble, but quickly focuses on two of them--Jaibo and Pedro. Jaibo is a burgeoning sociopath, and Pedro is just a kid who wants to be good but doesn't always succeed. Jaibo preys on Pedro, using him as an accomplice and victim.

reviews.text: Smooth brained butter harvested from deep within the final stroke ruined folds of some forgotten cryptid's grey matter that spent the better part of its life roaming the hillside forests subsisting on mushrooms, cheap wine, and yellowed dime store pulp. Alien dialogue, stilted and monotone, unruly characters with an inadvertent authenticity that makes them as comical as they are flamboyant and drugs, drugs, drugs. Not only does this film catch the elusive boom slip but it somehow manages to capture the whole sound guy, tape deck at his side, kneeling in the bushes, unexpectedly immortalized. Fuck it, film is expensive. Roll on, roll on. Does everything right but in the most lovingly wrong way possible. Grainy lighting, awkward stunts and violence, questionable edits. Implausible eye candy that entertains and confuses. Rightly seated in the pantheon of late night trash cinema. I crushed my copy and snort it daily as reminder that life is weird. Embrace it.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "They Call Me Macho Woman" is a 1989 action survival film directed by Patrick G. Donahue. reviews.text: I watched this early George Lucas joint in its hard-to-find original theatrical version. It's one of those dystopian sci-fis, set in a totalitarian future society where nobody's allowed to have individual identities or have sex, even though it's difficult to imagine a government ever coming to power on that platform. One of the worker drones, Winston Smith (Robert Duvall), ​takes the wrong pill, discovers sex, etc. In contrast to the fast-paced, childish, and escapist Star Wars, this is slow, self-consciously brainy, and Relevant with a capital R. In interviews, Lucas has always expressed a desire to make "abstract, non-narrative" cinema, and this is as close as he's gotten in feature-length form. It is a very effective and well-made mood piece,…

reviews.author: Sethsreviews
reviews.text: Very odd stuff. Throws you into these minimalistic wide settings for 80 minutes and creates such a distinct atmosphere. The blandness of the sets, functioning as almost characters in their own right, adding to the overall bleak impact. Full of strange retro-futuristic jargon - there are many absurd sections of dialogue, yet each one has its own bizarre appeal. A clear pre-Star Wars lesson for George Lucas on how to create a lived in sci-fi world with minimal resources. definitely worth the watch, especially considering it was his debut feature.

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: Watched the theatrical version for the first time - which almost feels like a different film? Maybe the only really great dystopia film, a non-derivative one, which asks us to consider a world where realities existence is uncertain. Reality becomes uncertain in a world oversaturated by images: Lucas doesn't posit a surveillance state, but a surveillance world. The idea of the technocracy here seems more allegorical for the times, but we also have to ask ourselves if it is possible that the image will become truly tyrannical. Lots of bits that call to mind the late Lucas works (the security officers are always stating "we want to help you") but what hits so much harder than the 2004 cut is…

reviews.text: I tend to award favorable ratings to innovative, ambitious projects, even if the quality falters somewhat due to what was being attempted. Hell, in the case of a film like Cloud Atlas I actually prefer ambition that is occasionally flawed over safe but seemingly flawless. Timecode, a film by Mike Figgis, is experimental and on paper fascinating so I knew it was the type of work that I absolutely had to see. During the entire duration of the film we are watching four screens at once, and this is because it is composed of four different cameras filming simultaneously for 90 minutes, no cuts and very little script to speak of with essentially the entire feature being improvised.

It is pure pulp, a dance of seduction and death between cinema’s toughest mannequin (William Petersen) and an ambiguous capitalist zombie (Willem Dafoe). A tale of bad crooks and even worse cops that plays against the usual hyper competence of the genre with a comic series of blunders and failure (I don’t think Petersen does a single thing that actually helps him catch Defoe the whole movie). It starts around Christmas but the only thing shared here is brutality and obsession. It is one…

reviews.text: Friedkin had a unique skill for finding Hell-on-Earth horror in just about any setting or genre, and doing so in this equally sleek and scorching piece of 80s neo-noir art-pulp transcendence—which takes an authentically researched counterfeit-printing crime procedural and stylistically pushes it to the surreal sensory overload of its unhinged, thrill-junkie hotshot cop protagonist—is still among his finest achievements. There's a lot in here to love but one of my favorite details is that brief flash cut back to the bridge bungee jumping in the middle of the astonishingly, recklessly tangible guerilla car chase through the LA river and reverse-traffic freeway. reviews.author: Luke Whitticase
reviews.text: It’s beyond frustrating that a film that looks this visually unique and imaginative can be such an arduous bore to watch. The film is 2 hours long and yet there’s only enough plot to last roughly half of this time. The rest is padded with meandering dialogue and distractions that completely deter from the story. In any other film I’d possibly appreciate the films dedication to spending time with its characters in smaller moments, but this is not a film that holds either the time or place for such lengthy insight. With the exception of the wide-eyed and child-like Joan Cusack, the cast are either wasted in their positions or speak way too often, be it through horribly undecided accents (Gambon) or just general irritation (Williams). I just don’t feel like there’s much of anything here for anyone to fully enjoy, and its themes are touched on more interestingly in plenty more, much better films.

reviews.text: Cogently, flawlessly Dante-esque satirical look at War in the age of Consumerism (note my Capital Letters: I Mean Business). State-subsidized war morphing into consumerism may register as overly simplistic and didactic, but in fact both the military and the toy manufacturers are fucking capitalist tools, a brilliant insight. Construction-tank metal becomes toy-metal plastic (THEY ARE NOT THE SAME), the catalyst for a generation of youth misunderstanding the napalm-istic impact of video games (unlike Barry Levinson, who Understands War and the horror of its trivialization). reviews.text: In which Bay hijacks a ludicrously expensive, mediocre toy commercial with a solid family blockbuster base by Spielberg and instead teaches millions of 10-year-olds the visual vocabulary of violent, racist military action movies. Still so funny to me that this was literally only conceived because Hasbro felt GI joe would be considered too controversial with the Iraq war under way and then greenlit Bay turning their children's space robots movie into one of the most jingoistic disaster movies of the Bush era. What's even funnier is that it's one of the better ones, operating on a level of visual sophistication only matched by how monumentally stupid it is. In other words: a perfect merging of material and maker. The soundtrack includes Linkin Park, Goo Goo Dolls, The Used, Smashing Pumpkins, Taking Back Sunday and Disturbed. We have to go back.

reviews.text: Famously a strike picture and filmed around its injured star, its authorship given almost exclusively over to Michael Bay. This is what happens when you let him jerry-rig a $200 million tentpole. Utterly shapeless mayhem, lurching, leaping from one explosion of excess to the next, blissfully and almost antagonistically unself-conscious, a diamond forced into existence by a Kryptonite-poisoned Superman's fist. Not only does this feature a gigantic parachute-farting alien robot disguised as a Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird, it is also packed with the as-yet-unrivaled densest, most ostentatiously near-abstract frames (and some of the most beautiful and plastic and destructive) of Bay's career, and it is a glorious cacophony of burning chrome, corporate manifest destiny, and shitty gay jokes. The finale takes place (and was actually filmed) atop the Great Pyramid of Giza, just because. This is what Milton meant when he wrote that the Devil saw how awful goodness was, except that Bay feels no loss of virtue to pine.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: True Grit, above all else, is surprisingly moving, embracing good messages to drive its dazzling adventure with potency and excitement. Rooster Cogburn is a man who takes no BS, constantly utilizing his aggressive and independent tone to intimidate others. However, Mattie Ross is a toughie, and will not let Cogburn get the best of her skillful power. These two form an everlasting bond that may have taken a bit to solidify, yet exemplifies the unlikelihood and distinctiveness of friendship. In a literal sense, it’s a revenge story; in a gratifying sense, it’s a story about developing companionships and surpassing your preexisting faith. Sure, the narrative itself is somewhat simple, but that classic, untouched 60s magic makes it all the more special.

Although it's a film that seems to have been caught between the old school whimsical style of the 40's and 50's and the new wave of Hollywood anti-heroes pioneered a year earlier by Sam Peckinpah with "The Wild Bunch" (especially in the Western genre).

reviews.text: Directorial perfection. Käutner's camera seems to glide towards emotion, almost Wellsian (with hints of Fassbinder) in the way a single shot can effortlessly navigate between multiple frames, each one perfectly composed, each one both enriching and informing the emotions on screen. Light seems to dance off the walls, shadows loom like ghosts, yet the film retains a startling intimacy in quiet moments of connection. And if this perfect concoction of framing, movement and mise-en-scene wasn't enough, Käutner also illustrates an intuitive understanding of montage, certain flashbacks rendered cinematic through a gorgeous barrage of energetic super-impositions - it's intoxicating cinema. The visual finesse here is all in service of a timeless story, one which seems to explore the way love, friendship…

reviews.author: James
reviews.text: not really that surprising (and faintly ironic even, given the history between Germany & France and all the chest-beating about the greatness of German art that was part and parcel with the Nazi regime) that the aesthetic inspiration for a talented and ambitious German filmmaker during the era of Nazism—an era where Deutschland alienated nearly all of its [incredible] homegrown artistic talent (coughArnoldSchoenberg&FritzLangcough) and enacted a near total vacuum within the arts—would be the French Poetic Realism. Happily though, Käutner jettisons the worst tendencies of that loose movement (overly determined fatalism, pessimism as pose, bad symbolism) and fills the space with corny humor and what I can only think to call a peculiarly German sort of weird, barbed sweetness.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Amazing to think this was made in the '40s at all, much less in the middle of the war in Germany. In its rule-ignoring, floating camera, its sparkling poetic realism, and its general feeling of being unstuck in time, it far more resembles the enduring early talkie works of filmmakers like Boris Barnet and Jean Renoir. In fact, in the plot's slow ramble over water on a tow barge, it even feels like Renoir's early silent, Nana. Though the war is never mentioned (the film might not even take place during it), you can feel it at the margins in the completely nonjudgmental depiction of the two friends vying for the same woman as all three navigate a profound loneliness…

reviews.text: This one has grown on me. Blatantly steals and broadly waters down its basic idea of dehumanizing militarization as genre machinery from some of the best actioners of the 80s (Rambo, Terminator, Robocop, etc) but Van Damme and Lundgren make for one hell of a pairing. Both have a stiff acting style that serves their re-animated Vietnam meatsacks, Van Damme the giant muscled innocent puppy dog and Lundgren the giant muscled genocidal psycho, together forming a dueling yin/yang of America's violent amnesia, its brutality and regret, coming back to blow up a gas station, diner, grocery store or farmhouse near you. The cherry on top is that Emmerich directs this with absolutely zero pretension, it's all kicking and grenades and squibs and one-liners... just pure 90s slomo fire & rain ownage that totally earns its R-rating.

A coincidence? I think NOT. This movie has not aged well at all, there's a lot wrong with it but it's so bat-shit, ridiculous and 80s that it kinda sorta ended up winning me over again on this rewatch. The man, the myth, the legend Bill Paxton has some great moments in this but the real reason to watch is Kelly LeBrock. She fucking owns every scene she's in. She's funny, gorgeous and otherworldly. Weird Science is pretty problematic and troublesome at times but it was fun and wacky enough to keep me entertained throughout.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: It’s almost redundant at this point to say ‘Angela Bassett as Tina Turner is one of the best performances ever’ but it’s true. The difficulty of putting the magic of her into words lies within the fact that it’s an experience rather than a calculated, predictable notion. Her screen time embodies such an emotionally rich and tough persona that it seems as if she is this woman. The amount of work, respect, energy and boldness she injects into each second is an unaltered treat that never fails to showcase the effects of both brutality and luck. Her musical numbers are impressively vibrant while her shocking realizations are beautifully haunting. The film may be a vehicle for her to succeed, but when it’s at THIS level, you can’t deny how absolutely entrancing she is.

reviews.author: Josh Larsen
reviews.text: Shortly before the bonkers climax of White God, a few impounded dogs alertly watch a Tom and Jerry cartoon called “The Cat Concerto” on a television set in their pen. Tom plunks away at Liszt’s Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2, as the dogs sit in rapt attention. It’s a darkly funny moment – especially given the carnage about to ensue – and also a perfect encapsulation of the movie’s aesthetic. A thrillingly wild mixture of high art and low, White God cheekily comments on how we often hide behind civilized culture to mask our basest natures.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Sort of like Ralph Bakshi's Dune or Excalibur. Taking some Tolkien-esque children's fantasy/sword-and-sorcery quest broad strokes and giving them that violent, horny, and political polemic edge that he's known for (nuclear anxiety, propaganda, militarism, fascism, the holocaust, etc) and coming out the other side as this surreal, gothic futuristic apocalypse with sexy fairies, Nazi orcs, a funky psych-rock soundtrack and a horny cigar-smoking wizard doing a Peter Falk impression. Not sure its mix of juvenile humor/fetishes and sober, hellish fairytale/anti-war messaging totally comes together but the trippy design work and crude expressionist animation (including rotoscoping of old war/battle movies) is pretty cool.

reviews.text: Andrea Arnold's Wuthering Heights is tactile and elemental, a stripped back adaptation that prioritises authenticity over melodrama. Wuthering Heights is my favourite novel and whilst this film's distinct style sets it apart from the text, I think it adequately captures key features of Emily Brontë's work. Unlike so many films, this so truly captures the Yorkshire moorland. You can almost feel the heather, the wind, the peat, and the loneliness. This is a film defined by its setting, one of dried autumnal ferns and dry stone walls. It's about the loneliness of the wilderness, which is perfect for the characters.

reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: Somehow one of my favorites of the Bond films despite being possibly the most overtly racist / orientalist. There is a certain 'commitment to the bit' that I overwhelmingly applaud in spite of occasionally coming too close to abject goofiness that threatens to tip the careful balancing of tone a pre-Craig Bond film requires. And until now the setpieces have always remained in the realm of the relatively-serious; here, the popularity of the franchise shows in the budget it's afforded and the assumed western audience's fascination with the 'Land of the Rising Sun' is supposed to excuse the ridiculous exoticist shenanigans that ensue. They don't for me, but the sheer scale of it all does.

reviews.text: the cold open, which sees a spaceship get eaten by another spaceship before cutting to Bond getting trapped in a Murphy bed and assassinated, had me lightly concerned this would fail to cohere in the same way as Thunderball. definitely on the goofier side but Connery is more of a straight man here, alternately bemused and bewildered by the strangeness of the plot in which he's entangled. this i think works better than the Bond who takes silliness fully in stride—he feels a little more real here. this is in one sense obviously quite racist but the Connerys also gesture at a kind of cross-national humanism that manifests in less condescending ways; the captured American astronauts chatting comfortably with their Russian counterparts while imprisoned ("In my country we're called cosmonauts") is practically globalist for 1967 mass entertainment. and Bond warming to Japanese culture when he learns that it is also incredibly misogynist? well that's kind of 60s globalism too.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: So this is my favorite one, though I wouldn't make an argument that it's the best. I could go on at length about its immaculate production design, the foregrounding of Ken Adam's work and his constant use of hard lines and angles in almost every surface (something director Lewis Gilbert, intentionally or not, contrasts with vulnerable human bodies at any available opportunity), or the then-cutting-edge mix of FX and practical stunts, setting a rhythm for Bond action scenes that would hold into the 90s. Well, you'll find nothing but sincerity here. None of your big budget sci-fi epics could ever feel half as alien as a single minute of Zardoz. Generally, people have a narrow view of what "good movies" look like, and this style of straight faced absurdity doesn't match. You don't have to love what Zardoz is doing, but I'm puzzled by the suggestions that it is incompetent. I'd argue this film executes what it's going for flawlessly.

reviews.text: The ultimate tropical nightmare jam—91 minutes of Fulci travelogue mixed with iconic grotesque gutmunching synched to the metronomic soundwaves of pulsating tribal beats courtesy of the great Fabio Frizzi, as Fulci immediately drops us into a Voodoo Undead Nightmare filled with sinewy flesh ripping, shark fighting, headshot hospital deaths, Molotov cocktails, THE eye gouge of the century, throat shredding, and rising conquistadors. reviews.text: Just experienced this the way Lucio Fulci intended it to be seen: low-rent smelly theater, faded-to-shit print, projectionist messing up, a screaming baby in attendance for some reason, and a preshow Looney Tunes short that seemed legitimately racist against Italians. reviews.author: John_Lehtonen
reviews.text: Post-narrative. This is not to confirm the common (mis)conception that Fulci is narratively inept (this idea is directly contrasted earlier in his career: Don't Torture a Duckling is a fluid network narrative decades ahead of the vogue; Beatrice Cenci cogently layers differing flashbacks, investigations, and personal reflections). Rather, Fulci here begins his radical stage (culminating in the films he'd make in the 1980s) of dismantling linear plot in order to explore ideas or aesthetics.

reviews.text: This is the greatest zombie movie ever made. When I think about the plethora of zombie films, television, and videogames I’ve taken in over the years, I realize that I’ve become somewhat numb to the genre. And yet, Zombie Flesh Eaters still feels fresh. Still stands out among the horde.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Other than the much talked about shark vs. zombie fight and the sun-stroked tribal island vibes Fulci isn't really reinventing the zombie genre here but his sensibility of slow-mounting dread, borderline surreal horror setpieces and too tangible gore FX works really well for it. He's patient with the reanimated movements as they rise from the dirt and heavily focuses on how repulsive they look, smell and feel. He rubs our faces in the gushing blood and torn limbs, and the wide-angle lens close-ups of their faces make sure there's no rotted texture, or wiggling worm we don't see. Also, has Fulci ever seen a beautiful actresses eye that he didn't then want to viciously gouge out with various objects lying around the set?
